a: These are the rules and the rulings
p: Chapters 12 to 26 are the core of Deuteronomy: the laws Moses lays out before Israel crosses the Jordan.
b: Chapters 12–26 are often called the Deuteronomic Code. They retell and rework many laws of the Covenant Code in Exodus 20:22–23:33 and of Leviticus, now spoken by Moses as a sermon to the people, full of "you" and of reasons to obey. The code opens and closes with the same pair, "rules and rulings" (12:1; 26:16). Most scholars connect some form of it with "the scroll of the law" found in the temple in the time of King Josiah (2 Kings 22:8–13), because Josiah's reforms follow its demands closely: one altar, no high places, a Passover at the temple (2 Kings 23). Traditional readers take the laws as Moses' own words. The book.json page sets out both views.
orig: הַחֻקִּים וְהַמִּשְׁפָּטִים (hachuqqim vehammishpatim), "the rules and the rulings"

a: under every leafy tree
p: The phrase becomes a stock charge in Kings and the prophets against worship at country shrines.
b: Hilltops and great trees were natural places of worship across Canaan. The phrase "on the hills and under every leafy tree" returns again and again in the books that follow: of Judah under Rehoboam (1 Kings 14:23), of King Ahaz (2 Kings 16:4), of the northern kingdom before its fall (2 Kings 17:10), and in Jeremiah, who pictures Israel lying down "under every leafy tree" like a prostitute (Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 3:6, 13). Hosea mocks sacrifices on hilltops under oak, poplar and terebinth "for the shade there is good" (Hosea 4:13). The adjective ra'anan means thick with leaves, fresh and full, rather than simply "green."
r: 1 Kings 14:23; 2 Kings 16:4; 2 Kings 17:10; Jeremiah 2:20; Jeremiah 3:6; Hosea 4:13

a: Burn their Asherah poles with fire
p: Asherah was a Canaanite mother goddess. Her symbol was a wooden pole or a living tree set up by an altar.
b: In the texts from Ugarit (about 1300 BC), Athirat is the wife of the high god El and mother of the gods. In the Bible asherah usually names a wooden object, cut down and burned (12:3; Judges 6:25–26) or "planted" (16:21), and sometimes the goddess herself (1 Kings 18:19; 2 Kings 23:4). Inscriptions on storage jars from Kuntillet Ajrud in Sinai (about 800 BC) bless people "by YHWH of Samaria and by his asherah," and a tomb text from Khirbet el-Qom near Hebron says much the same. Many scholars conclude that some Israelites worshiped the LORD together with Asherah, which is what this law forbids. Others think "his asherah" means the cult object at his shrine rather than a consort.

a: the place the LORD your God will choose
p: The book never names the place. Readers have identified it as Shiloh, Jerusalem, or a series of places over time.
b: The phrase "the place the LORD will choose" appears more than twenty times in Deuteronomy and Jerusalem is never named. Traditional Jewish and Christian readers see a promise fulfilled in stages: first at Shiloh, where God "first made my name live" (Jeremiah 7:12), then in Jerusalem, which God "chose" (1 Kings 8:16, 44; 1 Kings 11:36; 2 Kings 21:7). Critical scholars read the law as the program of King Josiah, who closed every shrine but Jerusalem's (2 Kings 23:8–9), written in a veiled way so that it could speak as Moses on the plains of Moab. The Samaritans read "has chosen" and identify the place with Mount Gerizim (see the variant on this verse). See the topic page.

a: to put his name there as its dwelling
p: Does the "name" stand in for a God who lives in heaven, or is it an old way of saying "to claim as his own"?
b: Gerhard von Rad and Moshe Weinfeld read this as "name theology": Deuteronomy corrects older ideas of God living in the temple. God himself is in heaven (26:15), and only his name dwells on earth, as Solomon's prayer puts it (1 Kings 8:27–30). Sandra Richter (2002) argued instead that lasum shemo sham, "to put his name there," matches an Akkadian phrase, shuma shakanu, which kings used when they set their name on a monument to claim a place as theirs. On her reading the verse says God will mark the place as his property, not that he is absent from it. Jewish tradition spoke of the Shekhinah, God's dwelling presence, resting in the temple.
orig: לָשׂוּם אֶת־שְׁמוֹ שָׁם לְשִׁכְנוֹ (lasum et-shemo sham leshikhno)

a: You will rejoice in everything you have put your hand to
p: Deuteronomy commands joy. Its worship is a family meal before God, shared with servants and Levites.
b: The verb samach, "rejoice," runs through these chapters (12:7, 12, 18; 14:26; 16:11, 14–15; 26:11). Most sacrifices here are eaten by the worshiper's household, not burned whole. The circle of joy always widens: sons and daughters, male and female slaves, the Levite, and in the feasts the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. The Talmud records the saying that "there is no rejoicing without meat" while the temple stood, and later "no rejoicing without wine" (Pesachim 109a). The phrase "everything you have put your hand to," literally "every sending of your hand," means all your work and its fruit.
orig: וּשְׂמַחְתֶּם בְּכֹל מִשְׁלַח יֶדְכֶם (usemachtem bekhol mishlach yedkhem)

a: each of us doing whatever is right in his own eyes
p: Moses describes life before the one altar. The book of Judges uses the same words for Israel's worst days.
b: Moses includes himself: "all that we are doing here today." In the wilderness and on the plains of Moab there was no single settled sanctuary, and worship was looser. The phrase returns as the refrain of the last chapters of Judges, where a man sets up his own shrine and hires his own priest: "In those days there was no king in Israel. Each man did what was right in his own eyes" (Judges 17:6; Judges 21:25). Deuteronomy's answer is not the king alone but "what is right in the eyes of the LORD" (12:25, 28).

a: the resting place and the inheritance
p: Rest in the land is the condition for the one altar. Psalm 95 and Hebrews 3–4 turn "rest" into a promise still open.
b: Menuchah is a place to settle down after wandering. The one-altar law takes effect when God will "give you rest from all your enemies" (12:10). Kings marks that moment with David (2 Samuel 7:1) and Solomon, who says at the temple's dedication that not one word of God's promise of rest has failed (1 Kings 8:56). Psalm 95:11 has God swear that the rebellious generation "will never come into my place of rest," and Hebrews 3–4 reads that oath to mean that "a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people" (Hebrews 4:9), a deeper rest still open. The same word names the "waters of rest" of Psalm 23:2.
r: 12:10; 25:19; 2 Samuel 7:1; 1 Kings 8:56; Psalm 95:11; Psalm 132:8, 14; Hebrews 3:11; Hebrews 4:1–11

a: the Levite who lives in your towns
p: In Deuteronomy the Levite is usually poor, living in other tribes' towns and depending on their gifts.
b: Levi received no tribal land (18:1–2; Numbers 18:20–24). Where Numbers pictures the Levites serving at the tabernacle and supported by the whole tithe, Deuteronomy pictures them scattered in "your towns" and needing care, so it lists them with the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow (14:29; 16:11, 14; 26:12) and warns, "do not abandon the Levite" (12:19; 14:27). Critical scholars link this to the closing of country shrines, which would have left local priests without work (compare 18:6–8 and 2 Kings 23:9). Judges 17:7–13 and Judges 19:1 show Levites wandering in search of a place.

a: you may slaughter and eat meat in any of your towns
p: Once worship moves to one place, Deuteronomy allows animals to be killed and eaten at home as ordinary food.
b: Leviticus 17:3–7 requires that an ox, sheep or goat be slaughtered at the tent of meeting, so that every meal of meat is also a peace offering. If there is only one altar, families far away could rarely eat meat, so Deuteronomy allows ordinary slaughter in the towns, with the blood poured out (12:15–16, 20–25). Jacob Milgrom and Bernard Levinson see Deuteronomy deliberately revising the older law. Traditional readers explain that the Leviticus rule fitted a camp gathered around the tabernacle, and this one fits a nation spread through the land. The Talmud records a debate over whether "meat of desire" had been forbidden in the wilderness (Chullin 16b–17a). "As they would a gazelle or a deer": game was never sacrificed, so this meat is like hunted meat.

a: for the blood is the life
p: Every law about meat in the Bible keeps one line: the blood belongs to God, because life is in it.
b: The ban goes back to Noah: "flesh with its life, its blood, you must not eat" (Genesis 9:4). Leviticus gives the reason: "For a body's life is in its blood" (Leviticus 17:11). Leviticus has hunted blood covered with dirt (Leviticus 17:13). Deuteronomy has it poured out "like water" (12:16, 24), treating it like any liquid given back to the ground. The apostles in Jerusalem kept the ban on blood for Gentile believers (Acts 15:20, 29). Jewish law drains and salts meat to remove the blood. "Hold firm" (chazaq) shows how strong the temptation was.
orig: כִּי הַדָּם הוּא הַנָּפֶשׁ (ki haddam hu hannefesh)

a: every abhorrent thing the LORD hates
p: The word covers both ritual and moral wrongs: idols, unclean food, cross-dressing, dishonest weights.
b: To'evah means something that disgusts or violates the order a person or a god lives by. The Egyptians found eating with Hebrews a to'evah (Genesis 43:32), and shepherds too (Genesis 46:34). In Deuteronomy the LORD calls many things to'evah: idols and child sacrifice (12:31; 13:14; 17:4; 18:9–12), forbidden food (14:3), flawed sacrifices (17:1), a woman wearing a man's gear (22:5), the fee of prostitution (23:18), remarriage to a divorced wife who has married another (24:4), and false weights (25:16). Proverbs uses it for liars and cheats (Proverbs 6:16–19; Proverbs 11:1). The KJV's "abomination" is right but sounds old.

a: They even burn their sons and their daughters in the fire
p: The Bible charges the Canaanites, and later some kings of Judah, with burning children. Archaeology is debated.
b: Kings Ahaz and Manasseh "made their sons pass through the fire" (2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6), and Jeremiah condemns the Topheth in the Hinnom Valley, where children were burned, "I never commanded it. It never came up into my heart" (Jeremiah 7:31). The king of Moab sacrificed his son on the city wall (2 Kings 3:27). At Carthage, a Phoenician colony, a sacred burial ground held thousands of urns with the burned bones of infants and young animals from about 750 to 150 BC. Lawrence Stager and others read them as sacrifices, as Greek and Roman writers claimed; Jeffrey Schwartz and others argue many were children who died naturally. See 18:10 and the topic on Molech.
r: 18:10; Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 3:27; 2 Kings 16:3; 2 Kings 21:6; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 19:5

a: Do not add to it, and do not take away from it
p: An old formula guarding a text. Revelation ends with the same warning. In Hebrew Bibles this verse is 13:1.
b: Deuteronomy says it twice (4:2 and here). Ancient rulers protected their laws and treaties the same way: Hammurabi's epilogue curses any later king who changes his words, and the Letter of Aristeas says a curse was laid on anyone who would add to or change the Greek translation of the Torah. Proverbs 30:6 warns, "Do not add to his words," and Revelation closes with a curse on anyone who adds to or takes away from "the words of the prophecy of this book" (Revelation 22:18–19). Rabbis read the rule as forbidding new commands presented as Torah, such as five tassels for four. Hebrew Bibles number this verse 13:1, so chapter 13 there runs one verse ahead.
orig: לֹא־תֹסֵף עָלָיו וְלֹא תִגְרַע מִמֶּנּוּ (lo-tosef alav velo tigra mimmennu)

a: a prophet or someone who has dreams
p: Prophets and dream-readers were known across the ancient Near East. The test here is what they ask you to worship.
b: Letters from Mari on the Euphrates (about 1770 BC) report to King Zimri-Lim the words of men and women who spoke for the gods and the dreams of ordinary people, sometimes with a lock of hair sent along to check them. In Israel God could speak through dreams as well as through prophets (Numbers 12:6; Joel 2:28). Jeremiah sets the two side by side and ranks God's word above dreams: "What has straw got to do with grain?" (Jeremiah 23:28). Chapter 13 does not ask whether the prophet's sign works; it asks where he leads. Chapter 18:20–22 gives a second test, for words spoken in the LORD's name.
orig: נָבִיא אוֹ חֹלֵם חֲלוֹם (navi o cholem chalom)

a: the sign or wonder he told you about comes true
p: A miracle does not prove a message. Jesus and Paul warn that false teachers will work signs too.
b: The law imagines a prophet whose prediction comes true and still must not be followed. So signs cannot be the final test; faithfulness to the LORD is (13:3–4). Jesus warns that "false messiahs and false prophets will arise and give great signs and wonders" to lead even the chosen astray (Matthew 24:24), and Paul and Revelation say the same of the lawless one and the beast (2 Thessalonians 2:9; Revelation 13:13–14). Maimonides drew a rule from this: Israel did not believe Moses because of his miracles, which could be doubted, but because they heard God at Sinai, so no miracle can overturn the Torah (Foundations of the Torah 8:1–3).

a: the LORD your God is testing you
p: The false prophet's success is allowed by God as a test, the same verb used of Abraham and of the manna.
b: Nasah, "test," is the verb of the binding of Isaac (Genesis 22:1), of the manna (Exodus 16:4) and of the wilderness years (8:2, 16). The test is of love "with all your heart and with all your being," the words of the Shema (6:5). Many readers find a hard question here: does God send deception? The text does not say God gives the sign; it says he uses the situation to show what is in Israel's heart. 1 Kings 22:19–23, where a lying spirit is sent to Ahab's prophets, raises the same question more sharply.
orig: כִּי מְנַסֶּה יְהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם אֶתְכֶם (ki menasseh YHWH eloheikhem etkhem)

a: hold on to him
p: The verb dabaq is the word for a husband holding to his wife in Genesis 2:24.
b: Six verbs pile up in this verse: follow, fear, keep, listen, serve, hold on. The last, dabaq, means to stick or cling. It is the word in Genesis 2:24, where a man "sticks close to his wife," and of Ruth, who "held on to" Naomi (Ruth 1:14). Deuteronomy uses it for loyalty to the LORD (4:4; 10:20; 11:22; 30:20). The Talmud asks how anyone can "follow," literally "walk after," the God who is "a consuming fire" (4:24), and answers from this verse: by walking in his ways, clothing the naked and visiting the sick as he did (Sotah 14a).

a: So you will sweep the evil out from among you
p: A refrain of Deuteronomy's laws on capital crimes. Paul quotes it to the church at Corinth.
b: U-vi'arta ha-ra' mi-qirbekha closes nine laws (13:5; 17:7, 12; 19:19; 21:21; 22:21, 22, 24; 24:7), and two more in the form "sweep the innocent blood out" (19:13; 21:9). The verb bi'er means to burn up or to clear away completely, as fire clears a field. The picture is of the community as a body that must be cleansed, since evil left alone spreads and brings guilt on everyone. Paul quotes the Greek form of the phrase when he tells the Corinthians to put out a man living with his father's wife: "Remove the evil person from among yourselves" (1 Corinthians 5:13). He turns a death sentence into exclusion from the church.

a: the friend who is like your own self
p: Assyrian loyalty oaths demanded the same thing: report any plotter, even a brother or son.
b: In 672 BC King Esarhaddon of Assyria made his vassals swear loyalty to his heir. The oath required them to report anyone who spoke against the crown prince, even his brothers or their own brothers, sons and daughters, or a prophet or an oracle-seeker, and never to hide it. Moshe Weinfeld and Bernard Levinson argue that Deuteronomy 13 borrows the form of such oaths and turns it toward the LORD as Israel's true king. The phrase "like your own self" (kenafshekha) recalls Jonathan, who "loved him as much as his own life" (1 Samuel 18:1), where the Hebrew is kenafsho, "like his own self." Jesus put loyalty to him above father, mother, son or daughter (Matthew 10:37).

a: Stone him with stones until he dies
p: For centuries Christians cited this chapter to execute heretics. Others answered that it belonged to Israel alone.
b: Augustine drew on Old Testament penalties when he defended forcing the Donatists back into the church (Letter 93). John Calvin's Defense of the Orthodox Faith (1554), written after Michael Servetus was burned in Geneva, argued from Deuteronomy 13 that rulers must punish false teachers. The Massachusetts Body of Liberties (1641) cited 13:6 and 13:10 in making idolatry a capital crime. Against this, the Anabaptists and Roger Williams, in The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution (1644), argued that these penalties belonged to Israel's covenant state alone and that the church's only sword is the word. Most Christians today read the chapter that way. The rabbis, for their part, hedged it with trial and witnesses (17:6) until it could hardly be carried out.

a: Some worthless men
p: The Hebrew is "sons of beliyya'al." By Jesus' time Belial had become a name for Satan.
b: Beliyya'al probably means "without worth" or "no use" (beli, "without"), though some link it to swallowing or to the underworld. It describes the men of Gibeah (Judges 19:22), Eli's sons (1 Samuel 2:12) and Nabal (1 Samuel 25:25). In the Dead Sea Scrolls Belial leads the forces of darkness against the sons of light, and Paul asks, "How can Christ be in tune with Beliar?" (2 Corinthians 6:15). The KJV's "children of Belial" keeps the Hebrew word as a name.

a: Put it under the ban
t: An Israelite town under the ban
p: The ban meant for Canaan falls on an Israelite town that turns to other gods. The rabbis doubted it ever happened.
b: Cherem, the ban (see 20:17), here turns inward: an Israelite town that worships other gods is treated like Jericho. Before acting, the people must "look into it, search it out, and ask questions with care" (13:14), three verbs of investigation. The Mishnah hedged the law with conditions: a majority of the town must have gone astray, and it must not be a border town, Jerusalem or a city of refuge (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:4–6; Sanhedrin 16b; Bava Kamma 82b). The Talmud reports the view that "there never was a town led astray, and there never will be," taught only for study and reward, though Rabbi Jonathan claimed he had sat on such a town's ruin-mound (Sanhedrin 71a). Judges 20, the war against Gibeah, comes closest in the Bible.

a: as a whole offering to the LORD your God
p: The burned town is like a sacrifice given wholly to God. The word recurs when Gibeah goes up in smoke.
b: Kalil means "whole, complete," and is used of an offering burned entirely (33:10; 1 Samuel 7:9). In Judges 20:40, when Israel takes Gibeah, "the whole of the city" (kelil ha'ir) goes up in smoke toward the sky, the same word. A tel is the mound left when a town is destroyed and later towns are built on its rubble; most ancient sites in the Middle East are such mounds. Here the mound must stay empty forever, like Ai (Joshua 8:28). Jericho's rebuilder was also cursed (Joshua 6:26; 1 Kings 16:34).

a: You are children of the LORD your God
p: Israel as God's son or children: a theme that runs from Exodus to Paul.
b: God calls Israel "my son, my firstborn" (Exodus 4:22), and Hosea remembers, "When Israel was a youth, I loved him, and I called my son out of Egypt" (Hosea 11:1), a verse Matthew applies to Jesus (Matthew 2:15). Here the people as a whole are God's banim, "sons" or "children," and that is the reason for the ban that follows: children of the living God do not mutilate themselves for the dead. Paul widens the circle: "as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are God's children" (Romans 8:14). Mishnah Avot 3:14 cites this verse: Israel is beloved, for they are called children of God.
orig: בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַיהוָה אֱלֹהֵיכֶם (banim attem laYHWH eloheikhem)
r: 32:5–6, 19; Exodus 4:22; Hosea 11:1; Jeremiah 31:9; Malachi 2:10; Matthew 2:15; Romans 8:14–16

a: Do not cut yourselves
p: Gashing the skin and shaving the head were common signs of grief among Israel's neighbors, even among the gods.
b: In the Baal myth from Ugarit, when the high god El hears that Baal is dead, he comes down from his throne, puts dust on his head, and gashes his cheeks, chin and arms. The prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel "cut themselves, as was their custom, with swords and spears" (1 Kings 18:28). Leviticus forbids the same rites for priests and for all Israel (Leviticus 19:28; Leviticus 21:5). Yet the prophets mention such mourning in Judah without comment (Jeremiah 16:6; Jeremiah 41:5; Amos 8:10), which suggests the law was not always kept. "Between your eyes" means the front of the head above the forehead.
r: Leviticus 19:27–28; Leviticus 21:5; 1 Kings 18:28; Jeremiah 16:6; Jeremiah 41:5; Amos 8:10

a: These are the animals you may eat
p: The food laws closely match Leviticus 11, with a list of permitted animals added and the swarming creatures left out.
b: Leviticus 11 and this chapter share the same tests (split hoof and chewing the cud; fins and scales) and nearly the same list of birds, often word for word in Hebrew. Deuteronomy adds the ten permitted animals of 14:4–5, drops the clean locusts and the land creatures that swarm (Leviticus 11:20–23, 29–38), and leaves out the rules about touching carcasses. It also opens with a heading of its own: "Do not eat anything abhorrent" (14:3). Jacob Milgrom argued that Deuteronomy abridges Leviticus; others think both draw on an older priestly list. On the hare and the hyrax, and on the pig, see the notes at Leviticus 11:5–7. The New Testament discusses whether these laws still bind (Mark 7:19; Acts 10:14–15).

a: the deer, the gazelle, the roe deer, the wild goat, the ibex, the antelope and the wild sheep
p: Only the first two names are certain. The rest are educated guesses from the Greek, the Targums and modern zoology.
b: Ayyal (deer) and tsevi (gazelle) are well known; Solomon's table included both (1 Kings 4:23). Yachmur may be the roe deer or fallow deer, aqqo the wild goat, dishon perhaps an ibex or addax, te'o an antelope (the KJV's "wild ox" follows the Greek), and zemer a wild sheep or mountain goat (KJV "chamois," which never lived in the region). All are wild animals that chew the cud and have split hooves, so they are clean, but they were hunted, not kept, and so were never sacrificed.
orig: אַיָּל וּצְבִי וְיַחְמוּר וְאַקּוֹ וְדִישֹׁן וּתְאוֹ וָזָמֶר

a: You may give it to the foreigner who lives in your towns
t: One rule for you, another for the foreigner
p: An animal that died on its own may be given to a resident foreigner. Leviticus treats it differently.
b: Deuteronomy forbids Israelites to eat nevelah, an animal that died without slaughter, because they are "a people holy to the LORD." The foreigner who lives among them (ger) and the foreigner from another nation (nokhri) are not under that call, so the meat may go to them as a gift or a sale, and nothing is wasted. Leviticus 17:15 instead says that anyone, "whether born in the land or a foreigner," who eats such an animal becomes unclean until evening and must wash. Scholars see two outlooks: Leviticus stresses one law for all who live in the holy land; Deuteronomy stresses Israel's special holiness. The gift itself shows care for a poor neighbor, the same people who share the tithe (14:29).
orig: לַגֵּר ... תִּתְּנֶנָּה ... אוֹ מָכֹר לְנָכְרִי (lagger ... tittenennah ... o makhor lenokhri)

a: Do not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother
t: The third time, among the food laws
p: Only here does the rule stand among food laws. The rabbis built the separation of meat and dairy on its three uses.
b: Exodus places this rule among harvest offerings (Exodus 23:19; Exodus 34:26; see the notes there on its possible origins). Deuteronomy sets it at the end of the food laws, which encouraged reading it as a law about what to eat. The Talmud reasons that the three repetitions forbid three things: cooking meat with milk, eating it, and profiting from it (Chullin 115b). The Mishnah extends the rule to poultry (Mishnah Chullin 8:1), later law required separate dishes, and custom set a wait of up to six hours between meat and dairy. Philo and Ibn Ezra saw in it a lesson in compassion, like the rule about a mother bird (22:6–7).
orig: לֹא־תְבַשֵּׁל גְּדִי בַּחֲלֵב אִמּוֹ (lo-tevashel gedi bachalev immo)

a: Year after year you must set aside a tenth
p: Numbers gives the tithe to the Levites; here the family eats it. Jewish tradition counted two or three tithes.
b: Numbers says, "To the descendants of Levi, look, I give every tithe in Israel as an inheritance" (Numbers 18:21). Here the farmer eats his tithe at the sanctuary and shares it with the Levite. Rabbinic law combined the two: a first tithe for the Levites (Numbers 18), a "second tithe" eaten by the owner in Jerusalem (this chapter), and in the third and sixth years of each seven a "poor tithe" instead of the second (14:28–29; Mishnah Ma'aser Sheni). Tobit 1:6–8 and Josephus (Antiquities 4.240) describe three tithes. Critical scholars think Deuteronomy and Numbers come from different times and places, and that one revised the other. See the topic on the tithe.
orig: עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר (asser te'asser), "tithe, you will tithe"

a: cattle, sheep, wine, beer, or anything else you would like
p: Shekhar is fermented drink, probably beer. The tithe is meant to be enjoyed.
b: Shekhar, usually "strong drink," is related to the Akkadian word for beer, shikaru; in the ancient Near East beer was brewed from barley and was a daily drink, though the word may cover date wine too. Priests on duty must not drink it (Leviticus 10:9), and a Nazirite gives it up (Numbers 6:3), but here a family on pilgrimage may buy it and drink before the LORD. Proverbs warns against drunkenness (Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 23:29–35), yet this verse treats wine and beer as part of a holy feast. The Hebrew of "anything you want" is "all that your nefesh asks": your appetite.
r: Leviticus 10:9; Numbers 6:3; Numbers 28:7; Proverbs 20:1; Proverbs 31:6; Psalm 104:15

a: When each three years come to an end
p: Every third year the tithe stays home in the town as food for the landless and the poor.
b: In the third year the tithe is not taken to the sanctuary but stored "in your towns" for the Levite, the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow. Deuteronomy 26:12–15 gives the prayer the farmer says when he has done it. The rabbis called it ma'aser ani, the tithe of the poor, and set it in the third and sixth years of the seven-year cycle. Amos mocks Israelites who brought their tithes too eagerly to the shrine at Bethel, "every three days" (Amos 4:4), perhaps playing on this law. It is one of the oldest known public welfare systems.

a: the foreigner, the fatherless and the widow
t: The three who have no one
p: Ancient kings boasted of protecting orphans and widows. Deuteronomy makes it every household's duty.
b: Hammurabi's epilogue says he wrote his laws so that the strong would not oppress the weak and so that the orphan and the widow would receive justice. The Ugaritic hero Danel sits at the city gate judging the cases of widows and orphans. Deuteronomy adds the foreigner who lives among them, with no land or clan, and turns the king's ideal into a law for every farmer: they share the tithe (14:29; 26:12), the feasts (16:11, 14) and the gleanings (24:19–21), and their justice must not be bent (24:17). God himself defends them (10:18). James echoes the trio: pure religion is "to visit orphans and widows in their trouble" (James 1:27).

a: you are to make a release
p: Did the seventh year wipe out debts, or only pause collection for a year? Jewish law took it as full cancellation.
b: Shemittah means "letting drop." In Exodus 23:10–11 the farmer lets his land drop, lying fallow in the seventh year. Here the lender lets his claim drop. Full cancellation is the plain sense of 15:9: lenders were tempted to refuse loans as the year drew near, which makes sense only if the debt would be lost. This is how the Mishnah and most commentators read it. A pause for one year, while the land rested and the farmer earned nothing, was suggested by S. R. Driver and some others. When people stopped lending, Hillel created the prozbul, a document handing the debt to the court, which the release did not cover (Mishnah Shevi'it 10:3–4).

a: because a release for the LORD has been proclaimed
p: Babylonian kings sometimes cancelled debts by decree. Deuteronomy puts the release on a fixed calendar, under God.
b: Old Babylonian kings issued misharum ("justice") edicts, often early in a reign, that cancelled certain debts and freed people sold for debt. The best preserved is that of Ammi-saduqa (about 1646 BC). Such releases depended on a king's goodwill and came at irregular times. Deuteronomy makes the release regular, every seventh year, and calls it "a release for the LORD": God, not a human king, proclaims it. Moshe Weinfeld connected these laws, the Jubilee, and the prophets' "proclaim liberty" (Leviticus 25:10; Isaiah 61:1; Jeremiah 34:8) with the ancient language of royal justice.

a: his neighbor, his brother
p: Deuteronomy calls every fellow Israelite a "brother," even the poor man, the debt slave and the king.
b: Ach, "brother," is one of Deuteronomy's favorite words for a fellow Israelite. The poor man is "your brother" (15:7, 11), so is the Hebrew slave (15:12), the man who finds your ox (22:1–4), the borrower (23:19) and the one who is flogged (25:3). Even the king must come "from among your brothers" and must not think himself above them (17:15, 20). The language turns a nation into a family. It is translated literally here because it carries the argument; modern versions often write "fellow Israelite." The law marks a boundary as well: the outsider is not a brother (15:3; 23:20).

a: Yet there will be no one in need among you
p: Verse 4 says there will be no poor; verse 11 says the poor will never cease. The early church quoted verse 4.
b: The two verses stand a few lines apart. Verse 4 states God's goal: if Israel obeys, blessing and the release will leave no one in need. Verse 11 states the fact: in the real world, "there will never stop being people in need," and so the command to give stands. Some read verse 4 as "there should be no poor among you." Luke seems to describe the first believers fulfilling it: "there was not anyone in need among them," because owners sold land and shared (Acts 4:34). Jesus quotes verse 11 when his disciples complain about a costly gift (see 15:11).
orig: אֶפֶס כִּי לֹא יִהְיֶה־בְּךָ אֶבְיוֹן (efes ki lo yihyeh-bekha evyon)

a: so that you turn cold toward your needy brother
p: The Hebrew says "your eye is evil toward your brother": a stingy, grudging look. Jesus uses the same idiom.
b: In Hebrew an "evil eye" is not a magic curse but meanness, a grudging attitude toward others (Proverbs 23:6; Proverbs 28:22), and a "good eye" is generosity (Proverbs 22:9). Jesus uses the idiom: "If your eye is evil, darkness will fill your whole body" (Matthew 6:23), and the vineyard owner asks the grumbling workers, "Is your eye evil because I am good?" (Matthew 20:15), which means "Are you envious because I am generous?" The "worthless thought" in the same verse is literally "a word of beliyya'al" (see 13:13).

a: For there will never stop being people in need in the land
t: "The poor you always have with you"
p: Jesus quotes this verse at Bethany. In context it is a call to give, not an excuse for poverty.
b: When a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus and some say it should have been sold for the poor, he answers, "For you always have the poor with you, and whenever you want you can do them good, but you will not always have me" (Mark 14:7; Matthew 26:11; John 12:8). His words echo this verse, whose next line is the command to "open your hand wide." Many readers point out that the saying, taken with its source, assumes that the hearers will keep giving to the poor. It has often been misused as a reason to accept poverty as normal.
orig: כִּי לֹא־יֶחְדַּל אֶבְיוֹן מִקֶּרֶב הָאָרֶץ (ki lo-yechdal evyon miqqerev ha'arets)

a: a Hebrew man or a Hebrew woman
t: The slave law of Exodus, revised
p: Exodus 21 freed the Hebrew man after six years; Deuteronomy includes women and adds gifts for the road.
b: Exodus says, "If you acquire a Hebrew slave, he is to work six years. In the seventh he goes free, owing nothing" (Exodus 21:2). Deuteronomy keeps the six years but makes three changes. It names the woman alongside the man, though Exodus 21:7 had said a daughter sold as a slave woman "does not go free the way male slaves go free." It requires generous gifts (15:13–14). And it drops the master's right to keep the wife and children he gave the slave (Exodus 21:4). Leviticus 25:39–43 goes further still: no Israelite should be treated as a slave at all. Jeremiah 34:8–17 reports a release under King Zedekiah that was proclaimed and then broken. The people involved were mostly debtors (see 15:1–2). See the topic on slavery.

a: sells himself to you
p: The Hebrew form can mean either. Was the slave sold by others, or did poverty make him sell himself?
b: Yimmakher is a Niphal form, which can be passive, "is sold," or reflexive, "sells himself." Leviticus uses the same form for a poor man who sells himself to a fellow Israelite (Leviticus 25:39, 47). Exodus speaks of the buyer: "If you acquire a Hebrew slave" (Exodus 21:2). A person could be sold by a creditor for debt (2 Kings 4:1), by a court to repay theft (Exodus 22:3), or by a father (Exodus 21:7). The rabbis distinguished a man sold by the court from one who sold himself, and gave them different terms (Kiddushin 14b). The Plain reads "sells himself," which fits the law's picture of a fellow Israelite pushed into service by debt.

a: Load him up generously
p: The rare verb comes from the word for "neck": hang gifts around his neck.
b: Ha'aneq ta'aniq lo uses a verb form found only here (the root appears once more as a verb in Psalm 73:6, where pride is worn "like a necklace"), from anaq, a necklace, or "neck." The picture is of loading the freed slave's shoulders with goods from flock, threshing floor and winepress, so that he does not start his free life with nothing. Some compare the Israelites leaving Egypt laden with silver and gold (Exodus 3:21–22; Exodus 12:35–36), which the next verse recalls. The Talmud debates the minimum amount (Kiddushin 17a). "As the LORD your God has blessed you": the gift should match the master's own prosperity.

a: put it through his ear into the door
p: Exodus has the ceremony "before God"; here it happens at the house door, with no mention of God or judges.
b: Exodus 21:6 says: "his master is to bring him to God. He will bring him to the door or the doorpost, and his master will pierce his ear with an awl." Deuteronomy keeps the door and the awl but leaves out "to God." Moshe Weinfeld saw this as part of the book's pattern of making older rituals ordinary once worship is centralized. Some Christian readers connect Psalm 40:6, "ears you have dug for me," with this rite of a servant who chooses to stay; Hebrews 10:5 quotes the Greek of that psalm. For the meaning of "for life," see the note at Exodus 21:6.

a: twice the pay of a hired worker
p: The Hebrew mishneh usually means "double." Some scholars read "the equivalent of" a hired worker's wage.
b: Mishneh sekhar sakhir is literally "a double of the wage of a hired worker." Many commentators explain that a slave worked day and night, or that his six years would have cost twice as much in wages. Isaiah speaks of "three years, counted the way a hired man counts his years" (Isaiah 16:14), as if a contract term were three years, so six years of service is twice such a term. Others read mishneh here as "the equivalent of," so the slave's work was worth a hired man's wages and the master has lost nothing. Either way, Moses argues with the master's purse as well as his conscience.

a: every firstborn male born in your herd and your flock
p: Numbers gives the firstborn animals to the priests. Here the owner eats them at the feast.
b: Numbers 18:17–18 says the firstborn of cattle, sheep and goats are sacrificed and their meat belongs to the priest. Here the owner and his household eat it "year after year" at the chosen place (15:20; 12:6, 17; 14:23). Rashi, following the Sifre, says this paragraph speaks to the priest, who eats the firstborn given to him. Critical scholars see two different systems, as with the tithe (see 14:22). The ban on working or shearing the firstborn treats it as already God's, before it is offered.

a: Keep the month of Abib
t: Abib, the month of new grain
p: Abib means fresh ears of barley, the spring month of March and April. Later Jews called it Nisan.
b: Aviv names barley in the ear, still green but full (Exodus 9:31; Leviticus 2:14). The month of Abib came in March to April, when barley ripened, and it begins the year in Exodus 12:2. After the exile the Jews used the Babylonian name Nisan (Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7). Deuteronomy gives only the month, not the day; Exodus 12:6 and Leviticus 23:5 set the Passover on the fourteenth. In modern Hebrew aviv means "spring," as in the city name Tel Aviv, "hill of spring." "By night" recalls Exodus 12:29–31.
r: Exodus 9:31; Exodus 12:2, 6, 29–31; Exodus 13:4; Exodus 23:15; Exodus 34:18; Leviticus 23:5; Nehemiah 2:1; Esther 3:7

a: from the flock and the herd
p: Exodus requires a lamb or kid. Deuteronomy allows cattle as well. Readers have explained the difference in two ways.
b: Exodus 12:5 says of the Passover animal: "You may take it from the sheep or from the goats." Deuteronomy says "from the flock and the herd," which includes cattle. Rabbinic readers kept the lamb for the Passover itself and took the cattle as the festival peace offerings eaten during the seven days (Pesachim 70b; Rashi). The Chronicler's account of Josiah's Passover lists both lambs and cattle (2 Chronicles 35:7–9). Critical scholars think Deuteronomy turned a family meal at home into a sacrifice at the temple, joined to the Feast of Unleavened Bread, so cattle could be offered like any sacrifice. Either way, the meal now happens "in the place the LORD will choose."

a: the bread of hardship
t: Lechem oni: "This is the bread of hardship"
p: The Passover Seder opens with these words in Aramaic. The rabbis played on oni as "poor" and "answering."
b: Lechem oni is "bread of affliction, misery or poverty." Unleavened bread recalls both slavery and the haste of leaving. The Haggadah, the script of the Passover meal, begins in Aramaic as the leader lifts the matzah: "This is the bread of hardship that our ancestors ate in the land of Egypt. Let all who are hungry come and eat." The Talmud reads oni two more ways: poor man's bread, so the matzah is broken as a poor man would break it; and bread "over which many words are answered" (onin), the telling of the story (Pesachim 115b–116a). "In a rush" is the word of Exodus 12:11; Isaiah 52:12 promises a new exodus that will "not go out in a rush."

a: You may not sacrifice the Passover in just any of the towns
p: In Exodus Passover is eaten at home, blood on the doorposts. Here it must be kept at the one sanctuary.
b: Exodus 12 pictures each family killing its lamb at home and marking the door. Deuteronomy moves the sacrifice to the chosen place, and the families "go back to your tents" in the morning (16:7). Kings records that King Josiah held such a Passover in Jerusalem, and comments: "No Passover like this one had been held since the time of the judges who led Israel" (2 Kings 23:22). In Jesus' day pilgrims crowded Jerusalem, where the lambs were slaughtered in the temple court and eaten in houses in the city (Mark 14:12–16). After the temple was destroyed in AD 70, Jewish families returned to a home meal, the Seder, without a lamb.

a: Cook it and eat it
p: Bashal usually means "boil," but Exodus forbids a boiled Passover. The word can mean "cook" in general.
b: Exodus 12:9 says: "Do not eat any of it raw, or boiled at all in water, but roasted over fire." Here the verb is bashal, often "boil." Yet Exodus itself has to add "in water" to make bashal mean boiling, which suggests the word alone can mean "cook" or "make ready," as it does of ripening grapes (Genesis 40:10). The Chronicler joined both texts: "they cooked the Passover in the fire" (2 Chronicles 35:13). Michael Fishbane and Bernard Levinson cite this as an early example of Scripture interpreting Scripture. See the note at Exodus 12:9.

a: Count seven weeks for yourself
t: Counting to the Feast of Weeks
p: Deuteronomy ties the count to the harvest, not to a date. Later Jews argued fiercely over when to begin.
b: Leviticus 23:15–16 counts fifty days "from the day after the Sabbath" when the first sheaf was waved. Deuteronomy says only to count from "the time the sickle is first put to the standing grain," a farmer's reckoning. Pharisees and Sadducees disputed which "Sabbath" Leviticus meant: the first day of the festival or the weekly Sabbath (Menachot 65a–66a). The book of Jubilees ties the feast to God's covenant with Noah (Jubilees 6:17–21), and later Jewish tradition linked it to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. The Greek name, Pentecost, means "fiftieth," the day the Spirit came on Jesus' followers (Acts 2:1). See the topic on the Feast of Weeks.

a: Hold the Feast of Booths for seven days
p: Deuteronomy names the feast for its booths but never tells anyone to live in them. Leviticus does.
b: The feast comes "when you gather in the harvest from your threshing floor and your winepress," which is why Exodus calls it the Feast of Ingathering (Exodus 23:16). Leviticus adds the branches and the command, "Live in booths for seven days" (Leviticus 23:42), as a memory of the wilderness. Deuteronomy stresses joy and sharing (16:14–15) and, every seventh year, a public reading of the law at this feast (31:10–13). When the returned exiles found the booth law written, they built booths, and "not since the days of Jeshua son of Nun had the Israelites done it this way" (Nehemiah 8:17). Jesus taught in the temple at this feast (John 7:2, 37–39).

a: Three times a year all your males are to appear before the LORD your God
p: The pilgrim calendar of Exodus is repeated, now at the one chosen place. Jesus' family kept it.
b: Exodus says: "Three times a year every male among you is to appear before the Lord, the LORD" (Exodus 23:17; Exodus 34:23). Deuteronomy adds "in the place he will choose" and names the three feasts, Unleavened Bread, Weeks and Booths. The rabbis called them the shalosh regalim, the three "foot" festivals, because people walked to Jerusalem. Women and children also went (16:11, 14; 1 Samuel 1:3–7), though only men were required. Luke tells us that Jesus' parents "would travel to Jerusalem for the Passover festival" year by year (Luke 2:41). On "appear before" or "see" God's face, see the note at Exodus 23:15.

a: Appoint judges and officials for yourself in all the towns
p: A court in every town and a higher court at the sanctuary. Chronicles credits a similar reform to King Jehoshaphat.
b: Exodus 18 has Moses appointing judges over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, and 1:9–18 retells it. Here every town has its judges and shoterim, officials or court officers; the word may come from a root meaning "to write," and the Israelite foremen in Egypt were shoterim (Exodus 5:6). Elders also judge at the gate (21:19; 22:15; 25:7). Chronicles says King Jehoshaphat of Judah (about 870–848 BC) "appointed judges in the land, in all the fortified cities of Judah" and set up a court in Jerusalem of priests, Levites and heads of families (2 Chronicles 19:5–11). Some scholars see the Deuteronomic law and that reform as related. See the topic on justice.

a: a bribe blinds the eyes of the wise
p: Repeated from Exodus 23:8, with one change: "those who see clearly" becomes "the wise."
b: Exodus 23:8 says that "a bribe blinds those who see clearly and turns the words of the righteous upside down." Deuteronomy keeps the second half and changes the first to "the eyes of the wise," a word from the world of wisdom teaching (compare Proverbs 17:23). Samuel's sons are the first judges accused of it: they "took bribes and bent justice" (1 Samuel 8:3). "Do not play favorites" is literally "do not recognize faces": do not let who a person is decide the case (1:17; Leviticus 19:15). God himself shows no favor and takes no bribe (10:17).
orig: כִּי הַשֹּׁחַד יְעַוֵּר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים (ki hashochad ye'avver einei chakhamim)

a: Justice, justice is what you must pursue
p: The doubled word is one of the best-known lines in Jewish ethics. The rabbis asked why it is said twice.
b: Tsedeq tsedeq tirdof: the noun is repeated for emphasis, "justice, only justice," and the verb radaf means to chase, as one chases an enemy. The Talmud gives several readings of the repetition: one "justice" for a ruling by law, one for a fair compromise; or, pursue justice by seeking out a good court and wise judges (Sanhedrin 32b). Others say it means just ends must be pursued by just means. The verse has become a motto for Jewish involvement in law and social action, and it was quoted in the American civil rights movement. The word tsedeq also means "right" and "righteousness"; it is rendered "right judgment" in 16:18. The "justice" of 16:19, "Do not bend justice," is a different word, mishpat, a ruling or the right a person is due.

a: do not set up a standing stone, which the LORD your God hates
p: Jacob and Moses set up standing stones for the LORD. Here God hates them. Archaeology shows them at Israelite shrines.
b: Jacob set up a matsevah at Bethel and poured oil on it (Genesis 28:18), and Moses built an altar "with twelve standing stones for the twelve tribes of Israel" (Exodus 24:4). Isaiah even foresees "a standing stone to the LORD" at Egypt's border (Isaiah 19:19). Deuteronomy now bans them beside the LORD's altar, because the Canaanites used them (7:5; 12:3). At the Iron Age fortress of Arad, in the Negev, archaeologists found a small Israelite temple with an altar and, in its inner room, a standing stone, apparently put out of use later. Critical scholars see in this law a later reform; traditional readers distinguish memorial stones from objects of worship.
r: 7:5; 12:3; Genesis 28:18–22; Genesis 31:45; Exodus 23:24; Exodus 24:4; Leviticus 26:1; Hosea 3:4; Isaiah 19:19

a: which I did not command
p: A strong understatement: God never ordered this worship. Jeremiah uses the same words of child sacrifice.
b: Moses suddenly speaks in God's voice: "which I did not command." The phrase is an understatement for "which I forbade." Jeremiah repeats it of the child sacrifices at Topheth and to Baal, "which I did not command, and I did not speak, and it never came up into my heart" (Jeremiah 19:5; Jeremiah 7:31). Worship of "the sun, the moon and the army of the heavens" spread in Judah under Assyrian rule: Manasseh built altars "for all the army of the heavens" in the temple courts, and Josiah removed the horses and chariots dedicated to the sun (2 Kings 21:3–5; 2 Kings 23:4–5, 11). Deuteronomy 4:19 had warned against it.
r: 4:19; Jeremiah 7:31; Jeremiah 8:2; Jeremiah 19:5; 2 Kings 21:3–5; 2 Kings 23:4–5, 11; Zephaniah 1:5

a: on the word of two witnesses or three witnesses
p: One of the most quoted rules of the Torah. Jesus, Paul and Hebrews all cite it.
b: Numbers 35:30 had said that "one witness alone may not testify against anyone so that he dies," and 19:15 widens the rule to any case. The New Testament uses it often. Jesus tells a disciple to take one or two others to a brother who sins, "so that every statement may stand on the word of two or three witnesses" (Matthew 18:16). Paul warns the Corinthians that "every word will be established on the mouth of two or three witnesses" (2 Corinthians 13:1; compare 1 Timothy 5:19). John's Gospel cites it: "It is even written in your law that when two people testify, their testimony is true" (John 8:17). At Jesus' trial the false witnesses "did not agree" (Mark 14:56–59). Hebrews 10:28 recalls that the law's death sentence required it.
orig: עַל־פִּי שְׁנַיִם עֵדִים אוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה עֵדִים (al-pi shenayim edim o sheloshah edim)
r: 19:15; Numbers 35:30; Matthew 18:16; Mark 14:56–59; John 8:17; 2 Corinthians 13:1; 1 Timothy 5:19; Hebrews 10:28

a: The hands of the witnesses are to be first against him
p: Those who accuse must carry out the sentence first. Stephen's stoning and John 8 both reflect the rule.
b: The rule makes the witnesses carry the weight of their words: if they lie, they have blood on their hands. At Stephen's stoning, "the witnesses put their cloaks down at the feet of a young man whose name was Saul" (Acts 7:58), which fits this law. In John 8 Jesus answers those who brought a woman caught in adultery, "Whichever one of you has never sinned, let him throw a stone at her first" (John 8:7). Many readers hear this verse behind his words. The Mishnah describes the witness pushing the condemned man from a height before the stones (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4).
orig: יַד הָעֵדִים תִּהְיֶה־בּוֹ בָרִאשֹׁנָה (yad ha'edim tihyeh-bo vari'shonah)

a: too hard for you to judge
p: Hard cases go up to the sanctuary. The rabbis saw here the basis of the Great Sanhedrin.
b: Jethro had advised Moses to keep the "big matters" for himself (Exodus 18:22, 26). Now hard cases go to the priests and the judge at the chosen place. "Between blood and blood" may mean deciding whether a killing was murder or accident, or between two claims of bloodshed; the other pairs concern lawsuits and injuries. The Mishnah places the Great Court of seventy-one judges in the Chamber of Hewn Stone in the temple and treats a scholar who defies its ruling as the "rebellious elder" of 17:12 (Mishnah Sanhedrin 11:2–4). Christian readers sometimes compare the council of Acts 15.
orig: בֵּין־דָּם לְדָם (bein-dam ledam), "between blood and blood"

a: Do not turn aside from the word they tell you, to the right or to the left
t: "Even if they say right is left"
p: A famous rabbinic debate: must you obey the court even when it is wrong?
b: The Sifre says: "Even if they show you that right is left and left is right, listen to them" (Sifre Deuteronomy 154), and Rashi repeats it. The Jerusalem Talmud reads the other way: only "if they tell you that right is right and left is left" (Jerusalem Talmud Horayot 1:1). The verse became the main proof text for rabbinic authority. The Babylonian Talmud asks where God "commanded us" to light Hanukkah candles, a rabbinic rule, and answers: in "Do not turn aside" (Shabbat 23a). Christian readers have used the verse in debates about church councils and tradition.

a: I will set a king over me, like all the nations around me
p: Israel later asks Samuel for a king "like all the nations." Was kingship God's plan or a thing allowed?
b: In 1 Samuel 8:5 the elders say, "So now, set up a king for us to judge us, like all the nations," and God tells Samuel, "you are not the one they have turned down. Me they have turned down" (1 Samuel 8:7). The Talmud records both readings of this law: Rabbi Judah says appointing a king is one of three commands for entering the land, with wiping out Amalek and building the temple; Rabbi Nehorai says the passage only anticipates Israel's complaining (Sanhedrin 20b). Maimonides counted it a command; Abravanel argued monarchy was a concession. Critical scholars see a law written with the failures of Solomon and later kings in mind. See the topic on kings.
orig: אָשִׂימָה עָלַי מֶלֶךְ כְּכָל־הַגּוֹיִם (asimah alai melekh kekhol-haggoyim)

a: someone who is not your brother
p: The Mishnah tells how King Agrippa, of Edomite descent, wept when he read this verse in public.
b: The king must be one of Israel. The Mishnah describes the reading of Deuteronomy by the king at the Feast of Booths in the seventh year (31:10–13). When King Agrippa, probably Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great, whose family came from Idumea (Edom), reached "You may not put over you a foreigner," his eyes filled with tears. The people called out, "Do not fear! You are our brother, you are our brother!" (Mishnah Sotah 7:8). The Talmud judged their flattery harshly (Sotah 41b). The verse shaped Jewish hostility to Herod's line, and Edomites were "brothers" in a looser sense (23:7).

a: he must not get himself many horses
p: Solomon broke all three limits. The writer of Kings seems to tell his story with this law in view.
b: Kings reports Solomon's horses "from Egypt" (1 Kings 10:26–29), his seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines who "turned aside his heart" (1 Kings 11:3–4), and gold weighing 666 talents a year (1 Kings 10:14). Many readers think the writer of Kings measured Solomon by this law, point by point; critical scholars think the law itself was shaped by the memory of Solomon. Horses meant chariots, the tanks of the ancient world, and trust in them was a rival to trust in God (20:1; Psalm 20:7; Isaiah 31:1). No earlier verse records God saying "You must never go back that way again"; the nearest is Exodus 14:13, and 28:68 threatens a return to Egypt as a curse.

a: He must not take many wives for himself
p: The rabbis allowed a king eighteen. The Qumran Temple Scroll required one wife for life.
b: The Mishnah sets the king's limit at eighteen wives, from David's count (Mishnah Sanhedrin 2:4). The Temple Scroll from Qumran rewrites this law: the king may take no other wife besides the first, because she alone is to be with him as long as she lives (11QTemple 57:17–18). The Damascus Document cites "he must not multiply wives" against men of its day who took a second wife (CD 4:20–5:2). Some Christians, beginning with the church fathers, read the verse as pointing toward one wife. In Deuteronomy itself the danger named is that "his heart will turn aside," as Solomon's did (1 Kings 11:4).

a: a copy of this law
p: The Greek translated "a copy of this law" as "this second law," deuteronomion. The name stuck.
b: Mishneh hattorah hazzot means "a copy (or repetition) of this law." The Septuagint, the Greek translation made before Jesus, rendered it to deuteronomion touto, "this second law," and the Latin Bible followed with Deuteronomium, which gives the English name. The book is not a second, different law; it repeats and explains the covenant on the plains of Moab. The rabbis also called the book Mishneh Torah, and Maimonides gave that name to his code of Jewish law. The Mishnah says the king must write a Torah scroll of his own and carry it with him (Mishnah Sanhedrin 2:4). In 2 Kings 22 a scroll of the law found in the temple is read to King Josiah.
orig: מִשְׁנֵה הַתּוֹרָה הַזֹּאת (mishneh hattorah hazzot); Greek τὸ δευτερονόμιον τοῦτο

a: his heart will not be lifted up above his brothers
p: Unlike other ancient kings, Israel's king makes no laws and is a brother under the same law as everyone.
b: Ancient kings were lawgivers: Hammurabi presents his laws as his own gift from the gods. Israel's king in this law does nothing of the kind. He leads no army of horses, keeps no harem or treasury, and spends his time reading a law he did not write, "so that his heart will not be lifted up above his brothers." Bernard Levinson has called the passage "the first constitution": the king, the judges, the priests and the prophets (16:18–18:22) each have limited powers under the Torah. Others see an ideal that no king of Israel met, though Josiah came closest (2 Kings 23:25).

a: The Levite priests, the whole tribe of Levi
p: Deuteronomy says "the Levite priests" and never mentions Aaron's sons as a separate rank. Are all Levites priests here?
b: Hakkohanim halwiyyim, literally "the priests, the Levites," is Deuteronomy's usual phrase (17:9, 18; 24:8; 27:9). Leviticus and Numbers draw a sharp line: only Aaron's descendants are priests, and the other Levites assist them (Numbers 3:5–10; Numbers 18:1–7). Critical scholars since Julius Wellhausen read Deuteronomy as treating every Levite as a possible priest (18:6–7), a stage before Ezekiel 44:10–16 limited the priesthood to the sons of Zadok. Traditional readers take the phrase as "the priests, who are of the tribe of Levi," noting that Deuteronomy knows Aaron's priesthood (10:6) and here speaks of priests and Levites side by side. The Plain English says "Levite priests" and leaves the question open.

a: The LORD is their inheritance
p: Levi has no land because God himself is its share. The Psalms make this the prayer of every believer.
b: God told Aaron, "I am your portion and your inheritance among the Israelites" (Numbers 18:20). Joshua repeats it when the land is divided (Joshua 13:14, 33). Ezekiel applies it to the priests of the new temple (Ezekiel 44:28). The idea moved from a tribe to any faithful person: "The LORD is my portion and my cup" (Psalm 16:5; compare Psalm 73:26; Lamentations 3:24). In practice the Levites' "inheritance" was the gifts and offerings, and towns with pastureland (Numbers 35:1–8).
r: 10:9; Numbers 18:20–24; Numbers 35:1–8; Joshua 13:14, 33; Ezekiel 44:28; Psalm 16:5; Psalm 73:26; Lamentations 3:24

a: the foreleg, the two cheeks and the stomach
p: Leviticus gives the priest the breast and the right thigh. Here he gets the foreleg, cheeks and stomach.
b: In Leviticus the priest's share of the peace offering is the breast and the right thigh (Leviticus 7:31–34). This verse names different parts. The rabbis took it as a separate gift from animals slaughtered for ordinary meat, the kind of slaughter 12:15 allows away from the altar, and the Mishnah applies it to cattle, sheep and goats in the land and abroad, with or without a temple (Mishnah Chullin 10:1), though later custom outside the land varied. Critical scholars see two systems from different settings. In 1 Samuel 2:13–16 Eli's sons stab a fork into the pot and take what it brings up, or demand raw meat before the fat is burned: the kind of abuse fixed portions prevent.

a: If he comes with all his heart's desire to the place the LORD will choose
t: Country Levites at the central altar
p: Any Levite may serve at the chosen place. Kings says Josiah's country priests did not.
b: This law lets a Levite from any town serve at the central sanctuary with equal rights and equal shares (18:7–8). If Deuteronomy's demand for one altar closed the country shrines, this law would have provided for their priests. But when Josiah carried out the reform, "those priests of the high places never went up to the LORD's altar in Jerusalem. But they ate bread made without yeast with their brother priests" (2 Kings 23:9). Critical scholars see the Jerusalem priests resisting the law. Traditional readers answer that those priests had served at idolatrous shrines and were rightly kept from the altar, as Ezekiel 44:10–14 says.

a: besides what he gets from selling what came to him from his fathers
p: The Hebrew is unclear. It may mean family property, or a priestly arrangement handed down from the fathers.
b: The Hebrew levad mimkarav al ha'avot reads literally "apart from his sales upon the fathers." Most take it to mean that the Levite keeps any money from selling family property, perhaps a house in a Levite town (Leviticus 25:32–34), and still receives an equal share. Rashi, following the Talmud, read it of the priestly duty rotations set up by "the fathers," which priests traded among themselves ("you take my week, I take yours"). Others suggest an income from sacrifices sold by family. No reading is certain.

a: anyone who practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens or works sorcery
p: After child sacrifice come eight ways of learning the future or working power, almost every term the Bible has.
b: Qosem qesamim practices divination, by lots or arrows or a liver (Numbers 22:7; Ezekiel 21:21; 1 Samuel 15:23). Me'onen may read clouds or times (Leviticus 19:26). Menachesh looks for omens; Joseph's cup was used this way (Genesis 44:5). Mekhashef works sorcery (Exodus 22:18). In 18:11 the chover chaver "ties knots," casting spells; the one who asks an ov or a yidde'oni consults the ghosts of the dead or spirits that know things (see Leviticus 19:31); and the doresh el hammetim "seeks out the dead." Mesopotamian scholars wrote whole libraries of omens. Israel is to listen to a prophet instead (18:15).
orig: קֹסֵם קְסָמִים מְעוֹנֵן וּמְנַחֵשׁ וּמְכַשֵּׁף (qosem qesamim me'onen umenachesh umekhashef)
r: 18:11, 14; Exodus 22:18; Leviticus 19:26, 31; Leviticus 20:27; Numbers 23:23; 2 Kings 17:17; 2 Kings 21:6; Isaiah 47:12–13; Galatians 5:20

a: asks ghosts of the dead or spirits that know things
p: King Saul drove out those who called up the dead, then went to one in disguise.
b: Saul had removed the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things from the land (1 Samuel 28:3). Then, facing the Philistines and with no answer from God, he went at night to a woman at Endor who was mistress of an ov, and asked her to bring up Samuel (1 Samuel 28:7–25). Readers have argued ever since whether Samuel truly appeared, or a demon or a trick did. Isaiah mocks those who say, "Ask the ghosts of the dead and the spirits that know things," and asks: should a people not consult its God? Should they ask the dead on behalf of the living? (Isaiah 8:19). Josiah removed such practices (2 Kings 23:24).

a: Be whole with the LORD your God
p: Tamim means whole, without flaw. The Greek reads "perfect," the word Jesus uses in Matthew 5:48.
b: Tamim describes a sacrifice without flaw and a person whose loyalty is undivided. God told Abram, "Go about your life in my sight, and be whole" (Genesis 17:1). Here it means: trust the LORD alone, and do not hedge with diviners. Rashi explains: walk with him wholeheartedly and wait for him; do not probe the future, but accept whatever comes. The Septuagint translates teleios, "perfect, complete," and Jesus' words, "So you are to be perfect, the way your heavenly Father is perfect" (Matthew 5:48), use the same word, though in a different setting.
r: Genesis 6:9; Genesis 17:1; Joshua 24:14; Psalm 15:2; Psalm 18:23; Matthew 5:48

a: a prophet like me
t: Who is the prophet like Moses?
p: A line of prophets, one future prophet, or the Messiah? Jews, Samaritans and Christians read it differently.
b: Jewish interpreters such as Rashi read the singular as a series: God will raise up "prophet after prophet" in place of the diviners of 18:9–14; some named Joshua or Jeremiah. Qumran waited for "a prophet" alongside two messiahs (Community Rule 9:11), and its Testimonia text (4Q175) quotes 18:18–19 with other end-time promises. Samaritans added 18:18–22 to their text of the Sinai story in Exodus 20 and await the Taheb, a prophet like Moses. In the Gospel of John, crowds ask John the Baptist, "Are you the prophet?" (John 1:21) and say of Jesus, "This man truly is the Prophet" (John 7:40). Peter and Stephen apply the verse to Jesus (Acts 3:22–23; Acts 7:37). But 34:10 says no prophet like Moses had yet arisen. See the topic page.

a: Do not let me hear the voice of the LORD my God again
p: The prophet is God's answer to Israel's fear at Sinai: they could not bear to hear God directly.
b: At Sinai the people said to Moses, "Let it be you who speaks with us, and we will listen. Let God not speak with us, for fear we die" (Exodus 20:19). Deuteronomy 5:23–31 tells the same scene and adds God's approval: "What they have said is good" (18:17; compare 5:28). So a prophet is not a human invention like the diviner but God's own provision: a man who stands between God and the people as Moses did. Hebrews 12:18–25 contrasts the terror of Sinai with the voice of Jesus that now speaks from heaven.

a: I will put my words in his mouth
p: God says the same to Jeremiah at his call. Jeremiah may have seen himself as the prophet like Moses.
b: At Jeremiah's call God touches his mouth and says, "Look, I have set my words in your mouth" (Jeremiah 1:9). Jeremiah also protests that he is too young to speak, as Moses said he could not speak (Exodus 4:10), and he intercedes for the people as Moses did (Jeremiah 15:1). William Holladay argued that Jeremiah understood himself as the prophet promised here. Balaam, too, can only say "the word God puts in my mouth" (Numbers 22:38). Jesus says, "I did not speak from myself. The Father who sent me, he himself, gave me a command about what I should say" (John 12:49), which many read as an echo of "he will tell them everything I command him."
r: Exodus 4:10–16; Numbers 22:38; Isaiah 51:16; Jeremiah 1:6–9; Jeremiah 15:1; John 12:49–50; John 17:8

a: the thing does not happen or come true
p: A failed prediction marks a false prophet. But what about warnings that God withdrew when people repented?
b: This second test (after 13:1–5) concerns prophets who speak in the LORD's name. Jeremiah uses it against Hananiah: a prophet of peace "will be recognized" only "when that prophet's word comes true" (Jeremiah 28:9). Yet the test has limits that the Bible itself shows. Jonah announced that Nineveh would fall in forty days, and God relented when the city repented (Jonah 3:4–10); Jeremiah 18:7–10 says many prophecies are conditional. Ezekiel foretold that Nebuchadnezzar would take Tyre, and later admitted that he received little reward from it (Ezekiel 26:7–14; Ezekiel 29:17–20). So the rule works best for the false prophet's promises of safety.
orig: בְּזָדוֹן דִּבְּרוֹ הַנָּבִיא (bezadon dibbero hannavi), "with arrogance the prophet spoke it"
r: 13:1–5; Jeremiah 18:7–10; Jeremiah 28:1–17; Ezekiel 13:1–7; Ezekiel 26:7–14; Ezekiel 29:17–20; Jonah 3:4–10; 1 John 4:1

a: set apart for yourself three cities
t: Refuge cities instead of the altar
p: Exodus let a killer run to God's altar. With one altar far away, Deuteronomy provides cities in every region.
b: Exodus promised the accidental killer, "I will set aside a place for you where he can run for refuge" (Exodus 21:13), and the next verse speaks of the altar. Adonijah and Joab ran to the altar and grabbed its horns (1 Kings 1:50–53; 1 Kings 2:28–34). Moshe Weinfeld and Jacob Milgrom argued that once the local altars were closed, the refuge had to move to cities. Numbers 35 lists six cities, three on each side of the Jordan, and Moses names the eastern three in 4:41–43. Joshua 20:7–8 gives the western ones: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem, and Hebron. Deuteronomy adds the practical detail of roads and of placing the cities through the land so no one has far to run.

a: Prepare the road
p: The Talmud says the roads to the refuge cities were kept wide and marked at every crossroads.
b: The Hebrew takhin lekha haderekh is "make the road ready." The Talmud fills in the picture: the roads to the refuge cities were kept in repair and wide, and at every crossroads stood a sign reading miklat, miklat, "refuge, refuge," so that a man running for his life would not lose his way (Makkot 10b). The Mishnah adds that two scholars went with the fleeing man to talk to the avenger on the way (Mishnah Makkot 2:5). Dividing the land "into three parts" means placing the cities so that each region has one close at hand.

a: the iron head flies off the handle
p: The Hebrew says the iron "slips from the wood." The rabbis debated whether that meant the handle or the tree.
b: Venashal habarzel min-ha'ets is literally "the iron slips off from the wood." Most read "wood" as the axe handle. But the same word ets was just used for the tree being cut, so the Talmud records a dispute: the sages say the head flew off the handle; Rabbi Judah the Prince says a chip flew off the log and killed the man, and only that case counts as accident (Makkot 7b). The example itself is the point: a killing with no intent and no hatred, the kind of death that could happen to anyone at work.

a: Then add three more cities to these three
p: The extra cities were never set apart. Maimonides took the verse as a promise of the messianic age.
b: If Israel's territory grows to the full borders promised to the ancestors, three more refuge cities are to be added, making nine with the six of Numbers 35. The Bible never records this. The Sifre and later rabbis saw it as a promise for the future, and Maimonides used it as proof that the Torah itself speaks of the Messiah: since God does not command in vain, and the land never reached those borders, the verse must look to the days of the anointed king (Laws of Kings 11:2). Others read it simply as an "if" that Israel's history never met.

a: Do not move your neighbor's boundary marker
p: Moving a field marker was a way to steal land. Babylonians and Egyptians also treated it as a grave crime.
b: Fields were marked with stones or posts, easy to shift by night. Proverbs says, "Do not move an ancient boundary that your ancestors set up" (Proverbs 22:28; Proverbs 23:10), close to a saying in the Egyptian Instruction of Amenemope that also forbids moving the markers on the edges of fields. In Babylon, land grants were carved on kudurru stones covered with curses on anyone who moved them. Hosea compares Judah's leaders to "people who shift a boundary marker" (Hosea 5:10), and 27:17 curses the one who does it. Jewish law later used this verse (hasagat gevul) against unfair business competition.
orig: לֹא תַסִּיג גְּבוּל רֵעֲךָ (lo tassig gevul re'akha)

a: a witness bent on harm
p: The Hebrew is "a witness of violence," one who uses the court as a weapon. Exodus uses the same phrase.
b: Ed chamas is a witness whose testimony serves chamas, violence or lawless harm, the sin that filled the earth before the flood (Genesis 6:11). Exodus forbids becoming "a witness who serves violence" (Exodus 23:1); the Plain here says "bent on harm" for the same Hebrew, to fit a courtroom. Psalm 27:12 and Psalm 35:11 complain of false witnesses "breathing out violence." The word for what he accuses the man of, sarah, means turning aside or rebellion, the same word used for the false prophet's message (13:5).
r: 5:20; 13:5; Genesis 6:11; Exodus 20:16; Exodus 23:1; Psalm 27:12; Psalm 35:11; Proverbs 19:5

a: do to him what he plotted to do to his brother
t: The false witness gets the sentence
p: A lying witness receives the punishment he tried to bring on his victim. Hammurabi had a similar rule.
b: Hammurabi's first laws put to death a man who charges another with murder and cannot prove it, and a false witness in a capital case (Laws of Hammurabi 1–3). The Mishnah worked out the rule for edim zomemim, "plotting witnesses": they receive the sentence only if they are exposed before the accused is executed, a ruling the Sadducees disputed (Mishnah Makkot 1:6). In the Greek story of Susanna, added to Daniel, Daniel exposes two elders who falsely accused her of adultery, and the crowd puts them to death, giving them the very punishment they had planned for her (Susanna 61–62). This law closes the Ten Words' ban on false testimony (5:20).

a: life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot
p: The third time the formula appears in the Torah. Here it punishes a false witness by the harm he intended.
b: The formula appears in Exodus 21:23–25 for injuries in a fight and in Leviticus 24:19–20 for wounding a neighbor. Here it measures the penalty for perjury: the liar suffers what his lie would have done. In each place it limits revenge as well as requiring justice: no more than the harm. Jesus quotes the saying, "You have heard that it was said, 'Eye for eye and tooth for tooth,'" and tells his hearers not to resist the evil person (Matthew 5:38–39). On the rabbinic reading that the formula means money payments, see the notes at Exodus 21:24.

a: see horses and chariots, an army bigger than yours
p: Early Israel fought on foot. The law's first word on war is not tactics but trust.
b: Chariots were the fastest and most feared weapon of the Late Bronze and Iron Ages, and Israel's highland tribes had few (Joshua 17:16–18; Judges 1:19; Judges 4:3). The reason not to fear is the exodus: the God "who brought you up from the land of Egypt" had thrown Pharaoh's horses and chariots into the sea (Exodus 14:23–28; Exodus 15:1, 4). The Psalms sing the same faith: some boast in chariots and some in horses, "but we call on the name of the LORD our God" (Psalm 20:7). The king's limit on horses in 17:16 follows from it.
r: 17:16; Exodus 14:23–28; Exodus 15:1–4; Joshua 11:4–9; Judges 4:3, 13–15; Psalm 20:7; Isaiah 31:1

a: the priest is to come forward and speak to the army
p: Before battle a priest gives a speech that begins like the Shema: "Hear, Israel." The Mishnah records it.
b: In Israel's wars God was the commander, so a priest spoke before the officers did. Priests sounded trumpets in battle (Numbers 10:9; 2 Chronicles 13:12), Phinehas went with the army against Midian (Numbers 31:6), and the ark was carried into the field (1 Samuel 4:3–4). The Mishnah calls him "the priest anointed for war" and gives his speech, expanding these verses: do not be afraid of the clatter of shields or the trampling of horses, for the LORD goes with you (Mishnah Sotah 8:1). His opening, "Hear, Israel," echoes the Shema (6:4).
orig: וְנִגַּשׁ הַכֹּהֵן וְדִבֶּר אֶל־הָעָם (veniggash hakkohen vedibber el-ha'am)

a: Has anyone built a new house and not yet dedicated it?
p: A new house, a new vineyard, a new bride: the same three return as curses in chapter 28 and as excuses in Luke 14.
b: The three exemptions protect a life just begun. Their opposite is one of the curses of chapter 28: building a house and never living in it, planting a vineyard and never enjoying it, being promised a wife whom another man takes (28:30). Before a battle in 165 BC, Judas Maccabeus sent home men who were building houses, engaged, planting vineyards or afraid, "each to go back home, as the law says" (1 Maccabees 3:56). In Jesus' parable of the great banquet, the guests excuse themselves with a field, five yoke of oxen and a new wife (Luke 14:18–20), which some scholars read as a play on this law. The Mishnah says the exemptions apply only to wars of choice; in a commanded war "even a bridegroom goes out from his chamber" (Mishnah Sotah 8:7, citing Joel 2:16).

a: not yet enjoyed its fruit
p: The Hebrew says he has not yet "made it common": a new vineyard's fruit belonged to God until the fifth year.
b: The verb chillel means to make common, to move something from holy use to ordinary use. Leviticus 19:23–25 says the fruit of new trees is not eaten for three years, and in the fourth year it is "holy, a gift of praise to the LORD"; only in the fifth year may the owner eat it. A man who has planted a vineyard and not yet "made it common" has worked at least four years without tasting his wine. The same verb appears in 28:30. In other places chillel means to profane God's name (Leviticus 18:21).

a: Is anyone afraid and fainthearted?
t: Afraid of the enemy, or of his sins?
p: Rabbi Akiva took the coward literally; Rabbi Yose the Galilean said it meant a man afraid because of his sins.
b: Fear spreads: one man's melting heart can melt his brothers' hearts, as Israel's did at Kadesh (1:28). Gideon applied this law before fighting Midian, and twenty-two thousand men went home (Judges 7:3). The Mishnah records two views. Rabbi Akiva: it means what it says, a man who cannot face the drawn sword. Rabbi Yose the Galilean: it means a man afraid because of the sins he has committed, and the other exemptions were given so that such a man could leave without being shamed (Mishnah Sotah 8:5). Rashi follows the second view.

a: offer it peace
p: Did Israel have to offer peace even to the Canaanite cities? Rashi said no; Maimonides and Ramban said yes.
b: Verses 10–15 concern "cities that are very far from you" (20:15), and verses 16–18 the cities of Canaan. Rashi limits the offer of peace to the distant cities. Ramban and Maimonides hold that peace was offered to every city first, Canaanite cities included, if they would give up idolatry and accept Israel's rule (Laws of Kings 6:1). They point to Joshua 11:19–20, which says no city made peace except the Hivites of Gibeon, implying that others could have. The Jerusalem Talmud says Joshua sent three letters to the Canaanites: leave, make peace, or fight (Jerusalem Talmud Shevi'it 6:1).

a: forced laborers
p: A town that surrenders supplies labor gangs. Israel later did this to Canaanites, and Solomon to his own people.
b: Mas is a labor levy or corvée, work demanded by a ruler. The Gibeonites became woodcutters and water carriers (Joshua 9:21–27), and several tribes put Canaanites to forced labor instead of driving them out (Joshua 16:10; Judges 1:28–35). Solomon "drafted them as slave labor" (1 Kings 9:21) and also drafted Israelites for his building works (1 Kings 5:13–14), which led to the revolt in which his overseer of forced labor was stoned (1 Kings 12:4, 18). Egypt's treatment of Israel had begun the same way (Exodus 1:11).
r: Exodus 1:11; Joshua 9:21–27; Joshua 16:10; Judges 1:28–35; 1 Kings 5:13–14; 1 Kings 9:20–22; 1 Kings 12:4, 18

a: do not let anything that breathes stay alive
p: The law orders the ban on the Canaanite towns. Readers have answered it in at least four ways.
b: As written: God, the judge of all nations, used Israel to punish peoples whose guilt was "full" (Genesis 15:16), to keep Israel from their worship (20:18). As war rhetoric: Kenneth Kitchen, Paul Copan and others note that ancient war reports use total language loosely, and Joshua and Judges say many Canaanites remained (Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21–36). As late ideology: many critical scholars think the ban texts were written centuries later, when no Canaanites were left, as a sharp lesson about loyalty; archaeology does not show a single sweeping conquest. As challenged by later readers: Maimonides held that even the seven nations were offered peace and could stay if they accepted the basic Noahide laws (Laws of Kings 6:1–4), and some Christians read the wars spiritually, as Origen did. Defenders of the traditional reading also point to built-in exceptions: Rahab and her family, and the Gibeonites, were spared (Joshua 6:25; Joshua 9). See the topic page.
r: 7:1–5; 20:17–18; Genesis 15:16; Numbers 21:2–3; Joshua 6:21; Joshua 10:40; Joshua 11:19–23; Joshua 15:63; Judges 1:21–36; 1 Samuel 15:3

a: Is the tree of the field a human being, to come under siege from you?
p: Read as a question, the tree is not an enemy. The KJV read a statement: "the tree of the field is man's life."
b: The Hebrew ki ha'adam ets hassadeh can be read "for the man is the tree of the field," which the KJV smooths to "for the tree of the field is man's life," meaning people live on its fruit. Rashi reads it as a question, "Is the tree of the field a man, that it should go into the siege before you?", and most modern translations agree: the tree did not start the war, so do not punish it. Ibn Ezra rejected the question reading: the tree of the field is a person's life, since people live on its fruit, so cutting it down destroys your own food. The KJV follows his line, so the two medieval readings match the two English traditions. The rabbis built on this verse the principle of bal tashchit, "do not destroy": wasting anything useful, from food to clothing to lamp oil, is forbidden (Shabbat 129a; Maimonides, Laws of Kings 6:10).
orig: כִּי הָאָדָם עֵץ הַשָּׂדֶה (ki ha'adam ets hassadeh)

a: Only the trees you know are not fruit trees may you destroy
