p: Assyrian kings boasted of felling enemy orchards. Yet Elisha once told Israel to cut down Moab's good trees.
b: Felling an enemy's orchards and date palms was a common way to punish a besieged city; Assyrian kings such as Shalmaneser III recorded cutting down the orchards around Damascus. This law allows only trees that bear no food to be used for siege works. It stands in tension with 2 Kings 3:19, 25, where the prophet Elisha tells Israel and Judah to "fell every good tree" in Moab, and they do. Some scholars think Deuteronomy's rule is later; others note that the Moab campaign was a punitive raid, not a siege of a city Israel meant to keep.

a: measure the distance to the towns around the dead body
t: Who answers for a body in a field?
p: Hittite and Babylonian laws also made the nearest town or ruler answer for an unsolved killing.
b: Ancient law treated an unsolved killing as a danger to the whole region. Hammurabi's laws make the city and its governor pay the heirs if a man is killed in a robbery and the robber is not caught (Laws of Hammurabi 24). A Hittite law even measures distance: if a man is found dead in open country, the town within a set distance is responsible (Hittite Laws 6). Israel's law does not ask for money; it asks the nearest town's elders to clear the land of blood guilt before God. The Mishnah debates whether to measure from the body's navel or its nose (Mishnah Sotah 9:4), and says the rite was stopped when murderers became too many (Mishnah Sotah 9:9).

a: a valley with a stream that never runs dry, land that is not plowed or sown
t: An ever-flowing stream, or a rough valley?
p: Nachal eitan can mean a stream that never dries, or a hard, rocky valley. Either way the land is wild and unused.
b: Nachal is a valley with a stream that may flow only in the rainy season, a wadi. Eitan means "lasting" or "strong": so either a wadi with water all year (Amos 5:24 uses nachal eitan for justice that never stops flowing), or, as the KJV and Maimonides took it, a "rough" valley of hard ground. The site must not be farmed, and the Mishnah adds that it may never be sown afterward (Mishnah Sotah 9:5). Breaking the young cow's neck, rather than slaughtering it, shows it is not an altar sacrifice; the same act is used for an unredeemed firstborn donkey (Exodus 13:13).

a: wash their hands over the cow
p: The elders' gesture says "we are innocent." Pilate makes the same gesture at Jesus' trial.
b: Washing hands in public was a sign of innocence: "I wash my hands in innocence" (Psalm 26:6; Psalm 73:13). Matthew alone records that Pilate, seeing a riot starting, took water and washed his hands before the crowd, saying, "I am clean of this man's blood... That's for you to see to" (Matthew 27:24). Readers have often noticed the contrast: the elders here truly do not know the killer, while Pilate knows the man is innocent and hands him over. The elders' words, "our eyes did not see it done," mean they did not see it and did not let it happen.

a: make atonement for your people Israel
p: No blood touches an altar here. The rite carries the guilt away, and the elders pray God to cover it.
b: Kapper, "make atonement," usually involves blood on an altar (Leviticus 17:11). Here the young cow is killed far from any altar, its blood falls on wild ground, and the elders pray. David Wright groups this rite with the scapegoat and the bird released in the open (Leviticus 14:7; Leviticus 16:21–22): ways of moving guilt out of the community. The prayer asks God himself to "make atonement" or "cover" (Numbers 35:33 says land polluted by blood can be cleansed only by the killer's blood). The last clause uses the passive, venikkapper: "the blood will be atoned for." The rabbis read this verse as showing that "the dead need atonement" (Sifre on Deuteronomy 210), and 2 Maccabees, which Catholic and Orthodox churches hold as Scripture but Protestants and Jews do not, tells of a sin offering Judas sent to Jerusalem for fallen soldiers: "he had atonement made for the dead" (2 Maccabees 12:45).

a: you may see among the captives a beautiful woman
p: The law limits what a soldier may do with a captive woman. Readers differ on whether it protects or troubles.
b: In ancient war captive women were usually raped or sold. This law makes the soldier wait a full month, lets the woman mourn her parents, requires marriage, and forbids him to sell her or treat her as a slave if he later rejects her (21:13–14). Many Jewish and Christian readers see a humane limit on war: the Talmud says the Torah here "speaks against the evil inclination," allowing what it cannot stop in order to restrain it (Kiddushin 21b). Many modern readers, including feminist scholars, point out that the woman's consent is never asked, and that 21:14 says he has 'innah, "dishonored" or "humbled," her, a verb also used of rape (Genesis 34:2; 2 Samuel 13:14). Both observations are true to the text. See the topic on sexual violence.

a: She is to shave her head and do her nails
p: "Do her nails" is ambiguous. One rabbi said cut them; another said let them grow.
b: Ve'asetah et-tsipporneha is literally "she will do her nails." Rabbi Eliezer said it means to cut them, as shaving means cutting the hair; Rabbi Akiva said to let them grow, so as to make her unattractive while the soldier waits (Yevamot 48a; Sifre). The shaved head and changed clothes may be mourning signs, or signs of leaving her old people behind, like the cleansing of a person healed of skin disease (Leviticus 14:8–9). Either way the month of waiting gives the man time to change his mind and the woman time to grieve.

a: since you have dishonored her
p: The verb 'innah means to humble or shame. It can describe rape, but by itself it does not say force or consent.
b: 'Innah (a form of anah, "be low") means to humble, shame or mistreat. It is used of Egypt's oppression of Israel (Genesis 15:13), of Sarah's harsh treatment of Hagar (Genesis 16:6), and of sexual acts that dishonor a woman, whether forced, as with Shechem and Dinah (Genesis 34:2) and Amnon and Tamar (2 Samuel 13:14), or apparently consensual, as with the betrothed woman in town (22:24). In 22:29 it is used of the man who "seizes" a virgin. The site renders it "dishonor" each time and leaves force or consent to the context and the notes. Here it explains why the man owes the woman something: having taken her, he may not sell her.

a: one loved and the other unloved
p: The law sounds like Jacob's family: a loved wife, an unloved wife, and a father who favored the younger son.
b: "The LORD saw that Leah was the unloved one" (Genesis 29:31), using the same word, senu'ah ("hated" in the KJV, meaning loved less). Leah bore Reuben, the firstborn; Rachel, the loved wife, bore Joseph, to whom Jacob gave a double share through his two sons (Genesis 48:5, 22). This law would forbid a father from doing that out of preference. Chronicles explains that Reuben lost his birthright because he lay with his father's concubine (1 Chronicles 5:1–2; Genesis 35:22). Many readers see the law as a comment on the troubles of Genesis.
orig: הָאַחַת אֲהוּבָה וְהָאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה (ha'achat ahuvah veha'achat senu'ah)

a: a double share
p: The firstborn's double share is literally "a mouth of two." Elisha asks for the same from Elijah.
b: Pi shenayim, "a mouth of two," means two portions: if there are three sons, the estate is split into four parts and the eldest takes two. A Middle Assyrian law also gives the eldest brother two shares (Middle Assyrian Laws B 1). Elisha asks Elijah for "a double share of your spirit" (2 Kings 2:9), asking to be his firstborn heir. "The first fruit of his manhood" repeats Jacob's words over Reuben (Genesis 49:3).

a: a stubborn and rebellious son
p: Parents may not kill a son themselves; they must go to the elders. The rabbis said it never happened.
b: Ancient fathers often had power of life and death over children; Roman law gave the father such power. Here both mother and father must go to the elders, and the town decides. The charge is more than disobedience: "a glutton and a drunkard" (21:20; compare Proverbs 23:20–21) describes a grown son wasting the family's goods. The Mishnah narrowed the law until it could hardly apply (Mishnah Sanhedrin 8:1–5), and the Talmud says, "there never was a stubborn and rebellious son, and there never will be," though Rabbi Jonathan claimed he sat on one's grave (Sanhedrin 71a). The plain moral objection is old: Rabbi Shimon asked whether a son should really be stoned because he ate too much meat and drank too much wine (Sanhedrin 71a), and many modern readers, Jewish and Christian, say that no disobedience, however chronic, deserves death. Jesus' enemies called him "a glutton and a drunkard" (Matthew 11:19), and in Luke 15 the father runs to welcome his wasteful son.
r: 21:19–21; Exodus 21:15, 17; Leviticus 20:9; Proverbs 23:20–22; Proverbs 30:17; Matthew 11:19; Luke 15:11–32

a: a man who is hanged is cursed by God
t: Cursed by God, or an insult to God?
p: The Hebrew "a curse of God" can mean God curses him, or his body left hanging insults God.
b: The body was hung up after death as a public warning, as Joshua did with five kings (Joshua 10:26–27). Qilelat Elohim talui is literally "a curse of God is a hanged one." Cursed by God: the Septuagint, Paul and most modern versions. An insult to God: the Mishnah says a man was hanged for cursing God, and leaving him up repeats the insult (Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:4). Rashi offers a parable: two twin brothers, one a king and one a robber who was hanged; passers-by thought they saw the king. A human body bears God's image (Genesis 9:6), so leaving it exposed shames God. See the variant on this verse and the topic page.

a: his body must not stay on the tree overnight
p: John's Gospel says the bodies of Jesus and the two others were taken down before the Sabbath for this reason.
b: The rule to bury the same day was kept for Israel's enemies (Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:27). John reports that the Jewish leaders, "so that the bodies would not stay on the cross on the Sabbath," asked Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies removed (John 19:31). Josephus says Jews took down even the crucified before sunset (Jewish War 4.317). The apostles spoke of Jesus as one "whom you killed by hanging him on a tree" (Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39), using this verse's word, and Paul argued that by becoming "a curse for us" Christ bought us free from the law's curse (Galatians 3:13). The Temple Scroll applies the verse to traitors hanged alive (11QTemple 64:6–13).
r: Joshua 8:29; Joshua 10:26–27; John 19:31; Acts 5:30; Acts 10:39; Acts 13:29; Galatians 3:13; 1 Peter 2:24

a: do not hide yourself from them
p: Exodus says to return your enemy's ox. Deuteronomy says your brother's, and forbids looking the other way.
b: Exodus gives the law in its hardest form: "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey straying, you must bring it back to him" (Exodus 23:4). Deuteronomy speaks of "your brother" and adds what to do when the owner lives far away or is unknown: take the animal home, care for it, and return it when he comes looking (22:2). The key phrase, "do not hide yourself," names the easy sin of pretending not to see. The Mishnah builds a whole chapter of lost-property law on these verses, including when an item must be announced (Mishnah Bava Metzia 2). Many readers compare the priest and the Levite who "went past on the far side" (Luke 10:31–32).

a: A woman must not wear a man's gear
p: Keli gever may mean a man's weapons. Readers have linked the law to war, to pagan rites, or to the order of the sexes.
b: The two halves differ. A man must not put on a woman's simlah, a cloak or garment. A woman must not wear a man's keli, a word for any article, tool or weapon. Targum Onqelos translates "a man's armor," and a rabbi in the Talmud took it to mean a woman should not go out to war with weapons (Nazir 59a). Maimonides thought the law aimed at pagan worship, where men dressed as women before the goddess of love and women wore armor before the god of war (Guide 3:37). Others read a general rule to keep the sexes distinct, as the law keeps seeds and threads distinct (22:9–11). Christians and Jews today disagree about how it applies to modern dress and to transgender questions.

a: Do not take the mother along with the young
p: Is this law about mercy or simply God's decree? The rabbis argued, and one boy's story shook a sage's faith.
b: Moses promises the same reward as for honoring father and mother, a good and long life (22:7; 5:16). Ramban and Maimonides saw a lesson in compassion: a person must not be cruel even to a bird, or, as Maimonides added, take a mother in her distress (Guide 3:48). Yet the Mishnah silences a prayer leader who says, "Your mercy reaches to the bird's nest" (Mishnah Berakhot 5:3), because the commands are decrees, not only kindness (Berakhot 33b). The Talmud tells of a boy who climbed a tower at his father's word, sent away the mother bird, took the young, and fell to his death: both commands promised long life. One sage, Elisha ben Abuya, is said to have lost his faith over such a case (Kiddushin 39b; Chullin 142a). Jesus said not one sparrow falls apart from the Father (Matthew 10:29).

a: make a railing around your roof
p: Israelite houses had flat roofs used as living space. The owner answers for a fall.
b: Roofs were flat, made of beams covered with brush and packed clay, and reached by an outside stair or ladder. People dried flax on them (Joshua 2:6), slept on them (1 Samuel 9:25–26), walked and prayed on them (2 Samuel 11:2; Acts 10:9) and built booths there (Nehemiah 8:16). A low wall, ma'aqeh, kept people from falling. The owner who neglects it brings "blood guilt" on his house, as if he had shed the blood himself. The rabbis widened the principle: one must not keep a vicious dog or a shaky ladder in one's house (Bava Kamma 15b), and Jewish law uses this verse for many kinds of safety.

a: or the whole crop will become holy
p: The KJV says the crop will be "defiled." The Hebrew says it becomes holy, that is, forfeit to the sanctuary.
b: Pen tiqdash means "lest it become holy." A forbidden mixture is not made dirty; it is taken out of ordinary use, as if it belonged to God, and the farmer loses it. Leviticus 19:19 gives the shorter rule: "Do not sow your field with two kinds of seed." The Mishnah's tractate Kila'im ("Mixtures") works out the details, such as how far apart vines and grain must be. Jacob Milgrom noted that the sanctuary itself was full of mixtures, such as the priests' sash of linen and colored wool (Exodus 39:29), so mixing belonged to the holy realm and was kept out of daily life.

a: Do not plow with an ox and a donkey together
p: An ox and a donkey pull unevenly. Paul's warning about a yoke that does not match uses a Greek word from this law.
b: An ox and a donkey differ in size, strength and pace, and the weaker one would suffer under a shared yoke; the ox was clean and the donkey unclean (14:4–8). Philo and others read it as kindness to animals. When Paul writes, "Do not hitch yourselves to unbelievers in a yoke that does not match" (2 Corinthians 6:14), he uses the verb heterozygeo, "yoke with a different kind," a word the Septuagint uses in the law against mating two kinds of animals (Leviticus 19:19). Many readers think Paul had laws like this one in mind.

a: Make twisted tassels for yourself on the four corners
t: Tassels next to the mixture law
p: Numbers 15 gives the tassels their reason. This rule comes right after the ban on wool with linen.
b: Numbers tells the Israelites "to make tassels for themselves on the corners of their clothes" with a cord of blue-violet: "You will see it and remember all the LORD's commands" (Numbers 15:38–39). Here the tassels are gedilim, "twisted cords," on the four corners of the cloak. Because the verse comes right after the ban on wool and linen, the Talmud ruled that woolen tassels may be put on a linen garment (Menachot 39b–40a; Yevamot 4a). Jesus wore such a garment, and a sick woman touched its tassel (Matthew 9:20; Matthew 14:36); he criticized those who made their tassels long for show (Matthew 23:5).

a: I did not find the signs of her virginity
p: The "signs" were probably a bloodstained cloth from the wedding night. Some rabbis and scholars read it differently.
b: In many traditional societies the bride's family kept the sheet from the wedding night as proof that she was a virgin. The parents' evidence here is "the cloth" (22:17). Modern medicine knows that many virgins do not bleed, so such evidence can wrong an innocent woman. Scholars such as Tikva Frymer-Kensky and Carolyn Pressler also note the double standard: a bride's past can bring her death, while nothing is asked of the groom. Some rabbis read the verse as a figure: "they make the matter clear as a cloth," bringing witnesses (Ketubot 46a; Sifre). Gordon Wenham argued that betulim here means signs of a girl of marriageable age, a menstrual cloth showing she was not already pregnant. The law's main target is the husband who makes up the charge, perhaps to get back the bride-price; he is fined and loses the right to divorce her (22:19).

a: the young woman's father
p: In the Torah's scrolls the word for "young woman" is usually spelled like "boy." Readers have always read it as "girl."
b: Throughout this chapter the consonants spell na'ar, "young man," where the sense requires na'arah, "young woman." The Masoretes, who added the vowels, marked it to be read as feminine, a "perpetual Qere." The spelling occurs about twenty times in the Five Books (Genesis 24:14; Genesis 34:3), while the rest of the Bible spells the word with a final -ah. Most scholars think na'ar was an old spelling for both sexes, like hu for "he" and "she" in the Torah. It does not change the meaning. See the topic on Ketiv and Qere.

a: a hundred shekels of silver
p: A hundred shekels was twice the payment in 22:29 and over two pounds of silver.
b: A shekel weighed about 11.5 grams, so a hundred shekels was over a kilogram of silver, many years of a laborer's wages. Abraham paid four hundred for the cave and field at Machpelah (Genesis 23:15–16). The fine goes to the father, whose household was shamed, and the husband loses the right to divorce her. The penalty is double the fifty shekels of 22:29. Some scholars note that a man who falsely accused his wife of a capital crime should have received her death sentence under 19:19, and the law here is milder.

a: a disgraceful thing in Israel
p: Nevalah is a deed that breaks the basic decency of the community. The phrase marks some of the Bible's worst stories.
b: Nevalah comes from the word for a fool (naval), someone who acts as if there is no God (Psalm 14:1). "A disgraceful thing in Israel" is said of the rape of Dinah (Genesis 34:7), the crime at Gibeah (Judges 20:6, 10), Amnon's rape of Tamar, who begs him, "do not do this disgraceful thing" (2 Samuel 13:12), and Achan's theft (Joshua 7:15). Here the crime is a bride who has deceived her husband and family. Death "at the door of her father's house" makes the family share the shame. The harshness of this law troubles many readers, and the rabbis hedged it with conditions (Mishnah Ketubot 4:3; Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4).
r: Genesis 34:7; Joshua 7:15; Judges 19:23–24; Judges 20:6, 10; 2 Samuel 13:12; Jeremiah 29:23

a: both of them must die
p: The law punishes both partners equally. In John 8 only the woman is brought.
b: Leviticus says the man who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife "must be put to death, the man and the woman who commit adultery" (Leviticus 20:10). Deuteronomy agrees and does not name the method. The Mishnah prescribed strangling for a married woman and stoning for a woman only promised in marriage, as in 22:24 (Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:4; Mishnah Sanhedrin 11:1). When the scribes bring a woman to Jesus and say, "Moses, in the law, ordered us to stone women like this" (John 8:5), the man is missing, though this law requires both. Many readers see that as part of the trap.

a: overpower her and lie with her
p: The law presumes the woman resisted and treats rape like murder. Its test for the town case troubles many readers.
b: The law compares the crime to "a man who attacks his neighbor and murders him" (22:26): rape is violence, and the woman is a victim with "no sin that deserves death." In the open country the law assumes she "cried for help, but there was no one to rescue her" (22:27), giving her the benefit of the doubt. The town case (22:23–24) assumes that a woman who did not cry out consented. Modern readers point out that fear or force can silence a victim, and the rabbis themselves taught that the field and town are examples, not rules: if a woman in town was threatened, she is innocent, and in a field she may be guilty if she consented (Sifre). See the topic on sexual violence.

a: he seizes her and lies with her
p: Is 22:28–29 a case of force, or of a couple caught together as in Exodus 22:16? Both readings are widely held.
b: The seduction reading, held by many commentators, such as Carolyn Pressler, Gordon Wenham and Daniel Block, notes four things. The verb changes from hechziq, "overpower," in 22:25 to tafas, "take hold of, catch"; "they are found" is plural, as if both were caught; there is no "cried for help" clause, unlike 22:24 and 22:27; and the law closely matches Exodus 22:16: "If a man lures away a virgin who is not promised in marriage and lies with her, he must pay her bride-price and take her as his wife." The rape reading takes tafas as force, as in its use for seizing captives, and the NIV and NRSV translate "rapes her." On that reading many find it cruel to bind a victim to her attacker; others see protection for a woman who might never marry. The rabbis read the two laws together: she becomes his wife only if she and her father agree (Ketubot 39b). The Plain keeps "seizes" and "dishonored" to leave the question open.

a: He must not lift the wing of his father's cloak
p: A modest way to say "his father's wife." Ruth asks Boaz to spread the same "wing" over her. In Hebrew this is 23:1.
b: Kenaf is a wing or the corner of a garment. Spreading one's cloak over a woman meant taking her in marriage: Ruth says to Boaz, "Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant" (Ruth 3:9), and God says the same to Jerusalem (Ezekiel 16:8). So "lifting" a father's wing means taking what is his: his wife, here a stepmother. Reuben lay with his father's concubine (Genesis 35:22) and Absalom with David's (2 Samuel 16:22), both claims to power. Paul condemns a man who "has his father's wife" (1 Corinthians 5:1). Hebrew Bibles number this verse 23:1, so the verses of chapter 23 there run one ahead.
orig: וְלֹא יְגַלֶּה כְּנַף אָבִיו (velo yegalleh kenaf aviv)
r: 27:20; Leviticus 18:8; Leviticus 20:11; Ruth 3:9; Ezekiel 16:8; Genesis 35:22; 2 Samuel 16:22; 1 Corinthians 5:1

a: may enter the assembly of the LORD
p: A castrated man was barred from the assembly. Isaiah promised such men a lasting name, and Acts 8 shows one baptized.
b: The "assembly" (qahal) was Israel gathered as a people before God, for worship, war or decision. Men mutilated in this way, often servants made eunuchs at foreign courts, were kept out, perhaps because the body had to be whole, as with priests and sacrifices (Leviticus 21:17–21; Leviticus 22:24). Isaiah later answered this law directly: God promises eunuchs who keep his covenant "a hand and a name better than sons and daughters" in his house (Isaiah 56:3–5). In Acts an Ethiopian eunuch reading Isaiah is baptized by Philip (Acts 8:27–38). Jesus speaks of those who "made themselves eunuchs because of the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 19:12).

a: born of a forbidden union
p: The KJV says "bastard," but a mamzer is not simply a child born out of wedlock. Its meaning was debated early.
b: Mamzer appears only here and in Zechariah 9:6, where it seems to mean a mixed or foreign people. The Septuagint guessed "child of a prostitute." The rabbis defined it as the child of a union forbidden under penalty of death or being cut off, such as adultery or incest, not a child of unmarried parents (Mishnah Yevamot 4:13). Later Jewish law, troubled by punishing the child for the parents' sin, worked hard to avoid declaring anyone a mamzer. "Even to the tenth generation" probably means "never," as 23:3 says outright.

a: No Ammonite or Moabite may enter the assembly of the LORD
p: Ruth the Moabite became David's great-grandmother. Readers have long asked how that fits this law.
b: Moab and Ammon were cousins of Israel through Lot (Genesis 19:37–38). Yet Ruth the Moabite marries Boaz (Ruth 4:10) and becomes the ancestor of David (Ruth 4:17). The rabbis answered: "An Ammonite, not an Ammonitess; a Moabite, not a Moabitess" (Mishnah Yevamot 8:3). The law, they said, applied only to men, because men were the ones expected to bring bread and water to travelers (Yevamot 77a). Nehemiah read the law more strictly and used it to separate Israel from foreigners (Nehemiah 13:1–3, 23–27). Judith, a book Catholic and Orthodox Christians include in the Old Testament, tells of Achior, an Ammonite who stands "in the middle of all their people" (Judith 6:16), is circumcised, and "was joined to the house of Israel, to this day" (Judith 14:10). Many modern scholars see the book of Ruth as a gentle answer to such strictness: a Moabite woman shows more covenant loyalty than many Israelites.
r: Genesis 19:37–38; Ruth 1:16; Ruth 4:10, 17; Nehemiah 13:1–3; Matthew 1:5; Judith 6:16; Judith 14:10

a: hired Balaam son of Beor
p: Numbers says Moab's king sent for Balaam. This verse adds the refusal of bread and water.
b: In Numbers, Balak king of Moab "sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor at Pethor" (Numbers 22:5). The story of how God made Balaam bless instead of curse fills Numbers 22–24. Deuteronomy sums it up: "The LORD your God turned the curse into a blessing for you" (23:5). Numbers does not mention Ammon's failure to give bread and water, and Deuteronomy itself says Moab sold Israel food (2:28–29), which suggests these traditions grew in different ways. Nehemiah quotes this verse (Nehemiah 13:2), and the New Testament remembers Balaam as the prophet who loved a fee (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11).
r: Numbers 22–24; Joshua 24:9–10; Nehemiah 13:2; Micah 6:5; 2 Peter 2:15; Revelation 2:14

a: Never seek their peace or their good
p: "Peace and good" were words for a treaty of friendship. The verse forbids an alliance, not personal kindness.
b: Delbert Hillers showed that "peace" and "good" (shalom and tovah) are the technical terms for friendly relations in ancient treaties: to "seek the peace and good" of a nation was to make a pact with it. So the verse rules out a formal alliance with Ammon and Moab, not ordinary decency toward them. Ezra quotes the line when he forbids marriage with the peoples of the land (Ezra 9:12). Jeremiah, strikingly, tells the exiles to "seek the peace" of Babylon (Jeremiah 29:7).

a: Do not abhor an Edomite, for he is your brother
p: Edom descends from Esau, Jacob's brother. Egypt enslaved Israel, but first it gave them a home.
b: Moses once sent word to Edom: "Your brother Israel says this" (Numbers 20:14). Edom refused passage, yet Deuteronomy still forbids hatred toward a brother nation. Egypt is a surprise: the land of slavery is also the land where Jacob's family found food and shelter (Genesis 45–47). The memory of being "a foreigner in his land" runs through this book's laws (10:19; 24:22). Later prophets were much harsher toward Edom after it joined in Jerusalem's fall (Obadiah 10–14; Psalm 137:7).

a: something that happened in the night
p: A polite way to describe a seminal emission during sleep, which made a man unclean until evening.
b: Hebrew miqreh laylah, "a happening of the night." Leviticus says a man with an emission of semen must bathe and is unclean until evening (Leviticus 15:16). The war camp was held to the standard of the sanctuary, because God was present in it. David's men could eat holy bread only because they had kept away from women (1 Samuel 21:4–5), and Uriah refused to go home to his wife while the army was in the field (2 Samuel 11:11). The Dead Sea Scrolls' War Scroll applies the same rule to the final war (1QM 7).

a: Have a digging stick among your gear
p: Ancient law, and the Essenes, took this hygiene rule as a matter of holiness.
b: The reason given is not health but holiness: "the LORD your God walks about in the middle of your camp" (23:14). Josephus says the Essenes carried a small spade, dug a pit a foot deep, covered themselves with a cloak so as not to offend God's rays, and would not relieve themselves on the Sabbath (Jewish War 2.147–149). The Temple Scroll from Qumran puts latrines three thousand cubits outside the holy city (11QT 46). The rule had real benefits for a large army, where disease was often deadlier than battle.

a: something indecent
p: The same rare phrase returns in 24:1, the law of divorce. Its meaning there was fiercely argued.
b: 'Ervat davar is literally "nakedness of a thing," something exposed that should be covered. Here it plainly means human waste left uncovered in the camp. In 24:1 the same words give the reason a husband writes his wife a certificate of divorce. The school of Shammai read 24:1 as sexual misconduct; the school of Hillel read "something" broadly (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). Readers who want to understand 24:1 often start here, where the phrase means something offensive, not necessarily sexual.

a: Do not hand a slave over to his master
p: Most ancient laws punished anyone who sheltered a runaway. This law says to let him live where he chooses.
b: Hammurabi's laws ordered death for anyone who helped a slave escape or hid a runaway (Laws 15–16), and ancient treaties often required kings to return each other's fugitives. Deuteronomy turns this around. The Talmud offers several readings: a foreigner who has given up idolatry and come to the land; a slave sold to a master abroad; and, best known, a slave who fled from abroad into the land of Israel (Gittin 45a). Most modern scholars read it as asylum for slaves fleeing from foreign masters. Others see it as wider. In Paul's letter to Philemon, he sends a runaway, Onesimus, back "no longer as a slave, but as more than a slave: a much-loved brother" (Philemon 16). American abolitionists cited this verse against the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850.

a: a shrine woman
p: The KJV says "whore" and "sodomite." The Hebrew words mean "holy one." Whether cultic prostitution existed is debated.
b: Qedeshah and qadesh come from the root "holy." Tamar, sitting by the road, is called both a "prostitute" and a "holy woman" (Genesis 38:15, 21), and 23:18 sets the qedeshah beside "a prostitute's fee." Older scholars believed in "sacred prostitution" at Canaanite temples, based partly on Herodotus. Many scholars now, including Joan Westenholz and Stephanie Budin, argue that no clear evidence for it exists and that these were cult personnel of some kind, later blamed as prostitutes. The kings of Judah removed the qedeshim from the land and the temple (1 Kings 15:12; 2 Kings 23:7). See also Hosea 4:14.

a: the price of a dog
p: Is a "dog" here an animal or a man? Many read it as a name for a male cult figure.
b: Many scholars take "dog" as the male counterpart of the prostitute in the first half of the verse, matching the shrine man of 23:17. A Phoenician temple tariff from Kition in Cyprus (5th or 4th century BC) makes payments to the klbm, which many scholars read as "dogs," temple servants, though others read a word for a kind of worker and the meaning is disputed. "Dogs" are also "dogs" are outside the city in Revelation 22:15. The rabbis read it literally: money from the sale of a dog, or a dog given in exchange, may not buy an offering (Mishnah Temurah 6:3). Either way, money earned through what God calls abhorrent cannot honor him, a principle Judas's thirty pieces illustrate when the priests will not put them in the treasury (Matthew 27:6).

a: Do not charge your brother interest
p: Exodus and Leviticus forbid interest to the poor. Deuteronomy forbids it to any Israelite and allows it to foreigners.
b: Exodus says: "If you lend money to my people, to the poor one among you, do not act toward him like a debt collector. Do not charge him interest" (Exodus 22:25). Leviticus adds: "Do not lend him your silver at interest, and do not give him your food for profit" (Leviticus 25:37). The Hebrew neshekh is "a bite." Loans in Israel were mostly to the needy, not business investments, and Babylonian rates ran 20 percent on silver and 33 percent on grain. The church long banned all interest among Christians, while Jews, allowed to lend to foreigners by 23:20, were pushed into moneylending in medieval Europe. Calvin argued that moderate interest on business loans was lawful. See the topic page.
r: 23:20; Exodus 22:25; Leviticus 25:35–37; Nehemiah 5:1–13; Psalm 15:5; Ezekiel 18:8; Luke 6:34–35

a: do not be slow to pay it
p: Ecclesiastes echoes this law: better not to vow than to vow and not pay.
b: A vow promised a gift to God, often if he answered a prayer, as Jacob (Genesis 28:20–22), Jephthah (Judges 11:30–31) and Hannah (1 Samuel 1:11) did. The law does not require vows: "if you hold back from making a vow, you will not be guilty of sin" (23:22). But a vow once spoken must be kept. Ecclesiastes says almost the same thing: do not delay to pay a vow, because it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay (Ecclesiastes 5:4–5). Jesus warned against oaths that make light of one's word (Matthew 5:33–37).

a: you may pick the heads of grain with your hand
p: Jesus' disciples did exactly this. The Pharisees objected to the day, not the picking.
b: A traveler or worker could eat from a neighbor's field or vineyard, but not carry any away. The disciples "began to pick heads of grain and eat them" as they walked through fields (Matthew 12:1; Mark 2:23; Luke 6:1). The Pharisees did not accuse them of theft, which this law allowed, but of harvesting on the Sabbath. The Mishnah limited the right to hired workers eating while they worked (Mishnah Bava Metzia 7:2), while others, like Josephus, read it as open to any passerby (Antiquities 4.234–237).

a: He writes her a certificate of divorce
p: The KJV reads "then let him write her a bill of divorcement," as if Moses ordered divorce. The Hebrew sets out a case.
b: Verses 1–3 are one long "if": if a man divorces his wife, and she remarries, and the second marriage ends. Only in 24:4 does the ruling come: the first husband may not take her back. The KJV and some older versions turned the middle of the case into a command ("then let him write"), which made it sound as though Moses required divorce. That reading lies behind the Pharisees' question, "Why then did Moses command us to give a certificate of divorce?" Jesus answered that Moses "allowed" it because of hard hearts (Matthew 19:7–8). Most modern versions now read the passage as this site does.
orig: וְכָתַב לָהּ סֵפֶר כְּרִיתֻת (vekhatav lah sefer keritut)

a: because he has found something indecent in her
p: What grounds did this phrase allow? Two Jewish schools disagreed, and Jesus was asked to take a side.
b: The Mishnah records the debate. The school of Shammai said a man may divorce his wife only for unchastity, reading the key word as 'ervah, "indecency." The school of Hillel said he may divorce her "even if she spoiled his cooking," reading the word davar, "something." Rabbi Akiva said even if he finds another woman more beautiful, from "she does not find favor in his eyes" (Mishnah Gittin 9:10). When the Pharisees ask Jesus whether a man may divorce "for any cause" (Matthew 19:3), they are asking about Hillel's reading. Jesus' answer, "except for sexual immorality" (Matthew 19:9), is close to Shammai's but grounds marriage in creation (Genesis 2:24). See the topic on marriage.

a: a certificate of divorce
p: The certificate protected the woman: it proved she was free to remarry.
b: Sefer keritut means "a document of cutting off." Without it, a woman who remarried could be accused of adultery. Documents on divorce survive from Jewish communities in the ancient world, including marriage contracts from Elephantine in Egypt (fifth century BC) that let either spouse end the marriage, and a divorce document from Wadi Murabba'at near the Dead Sea (AD 71/72). The prophets used the image for God and his people: "Where are the divorce papers I gave your mother when I sent her away?" (Isaiah 50:1); Jeremiah says God gave faithless Israel one (Jeremiah 3:8). The Mishnah's tractate Gittin sets out how the document must be written.

a: may not take her back to be his wife after she has been made unclean
p: The law forbids remarrying a former wife after another marriage. Its reason has puzzled readers.
b: The woman is not called guilty, yet she "has been made unclean" for the first husband. Some think the rule prevented something close to legal wife-swapping or a husband profiting twice from a dowry. Raymond Westbrook argued that a husband who divorced her for "something indecent" kept her dowry, so he must not later gain from her again. Others think it discouraged rash divorce. Jeremiah builds a sermon on it: "If a man sends his wife away... will he return to her again?" Yet God invites faithless Israel to return (Jeremiah 3:1, 12). Islamic law has the reverse rule: after a final divorce, she may return to the first husband only after marrying another (Qur'an 2:230).

a: to bring joy to the wife he has married
t: A year for the new bride
p: A new husband was free of war and public duty for a year. The law speaks of the bride's joy.
b: The Hebrew vesimmach, as the Masoretes pointed it, means he is to make her glad, as the KJV's "cheer up his wife" also says; some versions follow another pointing, "rejoice with his wife." The war law already sent home a man who had become engaged (20:7), and Jesus' parable has a guest say, "I've taken a wife, and so I am not able to come" (Luke 14:20). The Sifre extended the exemption to building a road, supplying water, or other public duties. This is one of the few ancient laws that names a wife's happiness as its goal.

a: a pair of millstones, or even the upper millstone
p: Women ground grain each day between two stones. Without the upper stone, a family had no bread.
b: A household mill was a flat lower stone and a smaller upper stone (the "rider") pushed back and forth over it. Grinding was daily women's work, often before dawn (Exodus 11:5; Matthew 24:41), and its sound meant a town was alive (Jeremiah 25:10; Revelation 18:22). A lender who took the upper stone took a family's ability to eat, "taking a life as a pledge." The Mishnah extended the rule to anything used to prepare food (Mishnah Bava Metzia 9:13). Abimelech was killed by a woman who dropped an upper millstone on him (Judges 9:53).

a: If someone is found stealing a person
p: Exodus gives the same penalty. Paul lists slave traders among the lawless.
b: Exodus says: "Whoever steals a person must be put to death, whether he has sold him or the person is found in his hand" (Exodus 21:16). Deuteronomy speaks of a fellow Israelite and adds the formula "sweep the evil out from among you." The rabbis read the eighth commandment, "do not steal," as being about kidnapping, since property theft is treated elsewhere (Sanhedrin 86a). Joseph's brothers did exactly this (Genesis 37:28). Paul lists "slave traders" (andrapodistai, man-stealers) among those the law condemns (1 Timothy 1:10), a verse often quoted against the Atlantic slave trade.

a: Remember what the LORD your God did to Miriam
p: Miriam was struck with skin disease after speaking against Moses. The rabbis drew a lesson about gossip.
b: Numbers tells how Miriam and Aaron spoke against Moses, and then "there was Miriam, struck with a skin disease, like snow" (Numbers 12:10). She was shut outside the camp for seven days, and the people waited for her (Numbers 12:15). Placing her story beside the skin-disease law (24:8) teaches that the priests' rules applied even to the leader's sister. The rabbis read skin disease as a punishment for slander (lashon hara), from this pairing (Sifre; Arakhin 15b), and Jewish tradition counts "remember Miriam" among six things to remember daily.

a: do not go into his house to take his pledge
p: A pledge was security for a loan. The lender must wait outside and let the borrower choose what to bring.
b: Lenders took a pledge (avot) as security, often clothing or tools. Letting the creditor walk into a home and take what he liked would shame the debtor and endanger the family. This law keeps the home as the debtor's own. Job counts taking pledges unfairly among the sins of the wicked (Job 22:6; Job 24:3, 9), and Amos condemns those who "lie down on garments taken in pledge" beside every altar (Amos 2:8).

a: so that he can sleep in his coat and bless you
p: Exodus gives the same law. A farm worker's letter from the seventh century BC appeals to it.
b: Exodus says: "If you take your neighbor's coat to hold as security, give it back to him by sundown, because it is his only covering, the cloak for his skin. What will he sleep in?" (Exodus 22:26–27). A pottery letter found at Mesad Hashavyahu near Yavneh-Yam, from about 630 BC, records a field worker's complaint to an official: his garment was taken after he finished his quota of harvest, and he asks for it back. It shows that such laws were known and appealed to. Here the result is "righteousness for you": kindness to the poor counts before God.

a: righteousness
p: Tsedaqah here means a right deed toward the poor. Later Hebrew uses it for charity.
b: Tsedaqah usually means rightness or justice. Here it is the credit a person has before God for returning a poor man's coat. The same word is used of Abraham's faith, "he reckoned it to him as righteousness" (Genesis 15:6), and of the people's obedience in 6:25. In later Hebrew tsedaqah became the ordinary word for giving to the poor, and Daniel urges a king to break off his sins "by righteousness" and mercy to the oppressed (Daniel 4:27). Jesus' warning about "your righteousness" before others leads straight into giving to the needy (Matthew 6:1–2).

a: Pay him his wages each day, before the sun goes down
p: Leviticus gives the same rule. James and Jesus' parable both build on it.
b: Leviticus says: "The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight until morning" (Leviticus 19:13). Day laborers lived on each day's pay, "his heart is set on it." Deuteronomy includes foreigners explicitly (24:14). In Jesus' parable the owner calls the workers at evening to pay them (Matthew 20:8). James warns the rich that the withheld wages of their workers "cry out" and reach the ears of the Lord (James 5:4), echoing "he will cry out to the LORD against you." Malachi lists those who cheat workers among those God will judge (Malachi 3:5).

a: Each one is to be put to death for his own sin
p: Ancient laws sometimes punished a son for his father's crime. This law forbids it, and Kings cites it.
b: Hammurabi's laws say that if a builder's house falls and kills the owner's son, the builder's son is put to death (Laws 229–230). Deuteronomy forbids human courts to do this. When King Amaziah executed his father's murderers but spared their children, the writer of Kings quotes this verse as the reason (2 Kings 14:6). Ezekiel makes it a principle of God's justice: "The son will not bear the father's guilt" (Ezekiel 18:20; Jeremiah 31:29–30). Many readers contrast it with God visiting sin "on the children" (5:9); the rabbis answered that this applies only when children continue the parents' sin (Berakhot 7a).

a: forget a sheaf in the field
p: Leviticus leaves the edges and gleanings. Deuteronomy adds what the harvesters forget. Ruth gleaned under these laws.
b: Leviticus says: "do not harvest all the way to the edge of your field, and do not gather up what is left behind after your harvest" (Leviticus 19:9). Deuteronomy adds the forgotten sheaf and the olives and grapes left after one pass. Ruth asks, "Please let me go to the field and glean" (Ruth 2:2), and Boaz tells his men to pull out stalks for her on purpose (Ruth 2:16). Rashi notes that the blessing is promised even for a sheaf lost by accident, so how much more for a gift given on purpose. The Mishnah tractate Pe'ah works out the details.

a: He may give him forty blows, but no more
p: The rabbis stopped at thirty-nine to be safe. Paul received that number five times.
b: The limit protected the guilty man's dignity: he remains "your brother." The Mishnah set the count at thirty-nine, so that no miscount could pass forty, and required a doctor to judge how many the man could survive (Mishnah Makkot 3:10–11). Paul writes, "Five times I received from the Jews forty blows less one" (2 Corinthians 11:24), a punishment synagogue courts gave members. Middle Assyrian laws often added forty or fifty blows to other penalties, with no such limit or concern.

a: Do not muzzle an ox while it is threshing
p: Paul quotes this verse twice for paying ministers. Does it concern animals at all?
b: Threshing oxen walked over the grain or pulled a sledge across it, and the law lets them eat as they work. Paul quotes it: "Is it oxen that God cares about? ... Or is he speaking entirely for our sake?" (1 Corinthians 9:9–10), and again for paying elders (1 Timothy 5:18). Some readers take Paul to deny that the law concerns animals. Others note his argument runs from lesser to greater, the rabbinic qal vachomer: if God cares for oxen, how much more for workers. The verse's place among laws about people (25:1–3, 5–10) has led some scholars to think it was always a proverb about fairness. The rabbis applied it to human workers too (Bava Metzia 88b).

a: do a brother-in-law's duty to her
p: Judah told Onan to do the same duty. Ruth's story and a question to Jesus both build on it.
b: The Hebrew yabam is a husband's brother; Latin levir gives the English "levirate." Judah told his son, "Go in to your brother's wife. Do a brother-in-law's duty to her, and raise up offspring for your brother" (Genesis 38:8). Onan refused in secret. Ruth's story stretches the custom to a more distant kinsman, Boaz, who acquires Ruth "to raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance" (Ruth 4:10). The Sadducees used it to mock the resurrection: whose wife will the widow of seven brothers be? (Matthew 22:23–28). Hittite law (193) and Middle Assyrian law (A 33) knew similar customs. Leviticus 18:16 and 20:21 otherwise forbid marrying a brother's wife.

a: so that his name will not be wiped out from Israel
p: The first son counted as the dead man's heir. In Ruth, though, Obed is listed as Boaz's son.
b: A man's "name" lived on in his heirs and his land. The levirate son would inherit the dead brother's share, keeping the family property whole, which may be why the law speaks of brothers "living together" (25:5). Zelophehad's daughters sought the same thing by another route (Numbers 27:4). Yet the book of Ruth ends by listing Obed as the son of Boaz (Ruth 4:21), and the women cry, "A son is born to Naomi!" (Ruth 4:17). Scholars debate whether the rule was strictly followed or was more flexible in practice.

a: pull his sandal off his foot, and spit in his face
p: The widow publicly shames the brother who refuses. In Ruth, a sandal changes hands to seal a deal.
b: A sandal stood for a man's right to walk on and claim land: "On Edom I throw my sandal" (Psalm 60:8). Ruth describes an older custom: "a man pulled off his sandal and gave it to the other man. This was how a deal was witnessed in Israel" (Ruth 4:7). Here the widow pulls it off herself, and spitting in his face adds public disgrace (compare Numbers 12:14). The Mishnah describes the ceremony, chalitsah (Mishnah Yevamot 12). The Talmud preferred levirate marriage (Yevamot 39b), but medieval Ashkenazi authorities came to require chalitsah in its place, and it is still performed in Orthodox Judaism.

a: Cut off her hand
p: This is the one place the Torah orders a body part cut off as punishment. The rabbis turned it into a fine.
b: Assyrian law orders a woman's finger cut off if she injures a man's testicles in a fight, and more if both are destroyed (Middle Assyrian Laws A 8). Deuteronomy's penalty is unique in the Torah; even "eye for eye" was read by Jewish courts as money (Exodus 21:24). The rabbis read the verse two ways: as payment for the shame she caused (Sifre; Bava Kamma 28a), and as the law of the pursuer, that one may stop an attacker even at the cost of a limb. Jerome Walsh argued that kaf here means her groin and that the penalty was shaving it, a public shaming. Some readers see in the harshness a concern for a man's ability to father children, as in 23:1. Many modern readers object that the penalty is out of proportion, and it is the only mutilation the Torah orders.

a: two kinds of weights in your bag
p: Merchants carried stone weights in a pouch. A crook kept a heavy one for buying and a light one for selling.
b: Silver was weighed on a hand balance against stones. Many inscribed Judahite shekel weights from the eighth and seventh centuries BC have been found, and they vary enough to show how easy cheating was. Leviticus says: "Have scales that are right, weights that are right, an ephah that is right and a hin that is right" (Leviticus 19:36). Proverbs calls false weights abhorrent to the LORD (Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 20:10), using the same word, to'evah, as 25:16. Amos condemns those who make "the ephah small and the shekel large" (Amos 8:5).
orig: אֶבֶן וָאָבֶן (even va'aven), "a stone and a stone"
r: Leviticus 19:35–36; Proverbs 11:1; Proverbs 16:11; Proverbs 20:10, 23; Amos 8:5; Micah 6:10–11

a: he cut down from behind all the stragglers at your rear
p: Exodus tells of a battle. Deuteronomy remembers an ambush on the weak at the back of the line.
b: Exodus says simply, "Amalek came and went to war against Israel at Rephidim" (Exodus 17:8), and then: "I will wipe out, yes, wipe out the memory of Amalek from beneath the sky" (Exodus 17:14). Deuteronomy adds the reason the memory must last: Amalek attacked the faint and weary, "and he did not fear God." Saul's failure to carry out the ban on Amalek cost him the kingdom (1 Samuel 15). In Esther, Haman is "the Agagite," a descendant of Amalek's king (Esther 3:1). See the topic on Amalek.
orig: וַיְזַנֵּב בְּךָ (vayzanev bekha), "he attacked your tail"

a: wipe out the memory of Amalek
p: Remember, and blot out. Judaism reads it aloud yearly; many ask how a command to destroy a people applies today.
b: On the Sabbath before Purim, called Shabbat Zakhor ("Remember"), synagogues read these verses aloud, and Jewish law counts hearing them as a duty. The rabbis ruled that the Assyrian king Sennacherib had "mixed up the nations" (Mishnah Yadayim 4:4), so the old peoples can no longer be identified; many later authorities applied this to Amalek, so the command cannot be carried out against any people today. Many Jewish thinkers read Amalek as a name for the cruelty that preys on the weak. Many Christian readers struggle with the command itself, and some see it as a war ruling limited to its time. See the topics on holy war and Amalek.

a: Put it in a basket
p: The Mishnah describes the procession: an ox with gilded horns, flutes, and King Agrippa carrying his own basket.
b: The Mishnah tractate Bikkurim describes the custom in the Second Temple period. Farmers marked the first ripe fruit of the seven kinds of the land (8:8) with a reed. They gathered in a district town, slept in the open square, and walked to Jerusalem behind an ox with gilded horns and a flute player. Craftsmen in Jerusalem stood to greet them. At the temple mount, even King Agrippa carried his basket on his shoulder (Mishnah Bikkurim 3:1–8). The rich brought baskets of silver and gold; the poor brought willow baskets, which they gave to the priests with the fruit.

a: My father was a wandering Aramean
p: Who was the Aramean, and was he wandering, perishing, or being destroyed? The Passover Haggadah reads it differently.
b: Most modern readers take the father to be Jacob, who lived in Aram with Laban, the Aramean (Genesis 28:5), and took a wife from his mother's family. The word oved means wandering, lost, or perishing. The Targum, the Passover Haggadah and Rashi read the words as "an Aramean tried to destroy my father": Laban, who chased Jacob and would have harmed him (Genesis 31:23–29). The Haggadah makes this the text for the whole Passover story. The words are unusual, and the reading is debated. See the variant note.

a: He went down to Egypt and lived there as a foreigner, few in number
p: Gerhard von Rad called 26:5–9 Israel's oldest creed. Many scholars now doubt that, but it still sums up the story.
b: In 1938 Gerhard von Rad argued that this "small historical creed," together with 6:20–24 and Joshua 24:2–13, was the seed from which the whole story of the Torah grew, since it names the ancestors, Egypt, the exodus and the land but not Sinai. Later scholars found its language typical of Deuteronomy, so it is probably not older than the book. Yet it remains a remarkable prayer: a farmer tells his own history as "we" and "us," and turns a basket of fruit into thanks for the exodus. Genesis gives the promise behind it: "I will make you a great nation there" (Genesis 46:3).

a: pressed us down
p: The farmer's prayer uses Exodus' words: pressed down, hard labor, cried out, heard.
b: Compare Exodus: "however hard they pressed them down, that much more they multiplied" (Exodus 1:12); "They turned their lives bitter with hard labor" (Exodus 1:14); "The Israelites sighed from their labor and cried out" and "God heard their groans" (Exodus 2:23–24); "I have come down to snatch them out of Egypt's hand" (Exodus 3:8). The prayer gathers the whole exodus into five verses. The Passover Haggadah takes these verses phrase by phrase and explains each with other verses from Exodus, the core of the Seder's storytelling.

a: with a strong hand and an outstretched arm
p: Egyptian texts praise Pharaoh's "strong arm." Israel's prayer gives that power to the LORD instead.
b: James Hoffmeier noted that Egyptian royal inscriptions often describe Pharaoh as "strong of arm" or as the one whose arm defeats foreign lands. Exodus uses the same image when God says, "I will redeem you with my arm stretched out and with great judgments" (Exodus 6:6). Deuteronomy repeats "a strong hand and an outstretched arm" as a fixed phrase (4:34; 5:15; 7:19). The point is pointed: the arm that brought Israel out was stronger than the king who claimed the strongest arm. The Haggadah reads the "great terror" as the presence of God himself.
orig: בְּיָד חֲזָקָה וּבִזְרֹעַ נְטוּיָה (beyad chazaqah uvizroa netuyah)

a: Rejoice in all the good things
p: Deuteronomy's worship is joyful, and the Levite and foreigner always share the joy.
b: "Rejoice before the LORD" runs through the chapters on worship: at the central place (12:7, 12, 18), with the tithe (14:26) and at the feasts (16:11, 14). Each time the circle is wide: the household, the Levite who has no land, and the foreigner. Gratitude for the land is not complete unless those without land share it. Jesus' story of the banquet makes a similar point: invite the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind (Luke 14:13).

a: I have cleared the holy portion out of my house
p: The Mishnah calls this the "confession of tithes." The farmer declares he has kept the rules, not that he has sinned.
b: Every third year the tithe was kept in the towns for the poor (14:28–29). Afterward the farmer declared he had given it. The Mishnah says this was done on the last day of Passover in the fourth and seventh years, and that Yohanan the high priest, often taken to be John Hyrcanus, ended the declaration (Mishnah Ma'aser Sheni 5:10–15). The Talmud explains that since Ezra's time the first tithe had gone to priests, so a farmer could no longer truthfully say he gave it to the Levite (Sotah 48a). The word for "cleared" (bi'arti) is the same verb as "sweep the evil out," here used for removing what belongs to God from the house. Jewish tradition reads 26:5–10 and 26:13–15 as two of the Torah's few set prayers.

a: I have not given any of it for the dead
p: Offerings to the dead were common in Canaan and Egypt. The holy portion could not be used for them.
b: Neighboring peoples set out food and drink for their dead, and Ugaritic texts describe meals for the departed ancestors. Israel's tithe could not go to such rites or be eaten in mourning, a time of uncleanness (Hosea 9:4). Some readers think the verse forbids only offerings to the dead as divine. Others see a ban on any gift for a funeral. Tobit tells his son to "Pour out your bread on the grave of the righteous" (Tobit 4:17), which shows that such customs lived on in Jewish life. Rashi read "for the dead" as buying a coffin or shroud. See the topic on Sheol.

a: Look down from your holy dwelling, from the heavens
p: God makes his name live at the chosen place, but he dwells in heaven. Solomon's prayer says the same.
b: Deuteronomy speaks carefully: God's name lives at the place he chooses (12:5, 11; 26:2), but God himself dwells in the heavens. Solomon prays at the temple's dedication that God would hear "in heaven your dwelling place" (1 Kings 8:30, 39, 43), and asks whether heaven itself can contain him (1 Kings 8:27). Isaiah's prayer asks God to "look down from heaven and see" (Isaiah 63:15). Many scholars call this Deuteronomy's "name theology"; Sandra Richter argued that the phrase means to claim the place, as a king inscribed his name.

a: Today you have affirmed
p: The verb he'emir appears only here and in 26:18. The two verses read like the two sides of a contract.
b: He'emarta and he'emirkha are a rare form of the verb "say," found only in these two verses. It probably means "caused to say" or "declared," as in a formal agreement: Israel declares that the LORD is its God; the LORD declares that Israel is his people. Many scholars see a marriage or treaty formula, the two sides of "I will be your God, and you will be my people" (Leviticus 26:12). The KJV's "avouched" captured the solemn tone. Some read the verb as "made the LORD say" instead, so the covenant is a mutual exchange of promises.

a: a people holy to the LORD your God
p: The law code ends where Sinai began. Peter applies the same words to the church.
b: At Sinai God said, "out of all the peoples you will be my own private treasure," and "you will be for me a kingdom of priests, a holy nation" (Exodus 19:5–6). Deuteronomy returns to those words (7:6; 14:2) and here closes the law code with them. Israel is set "high above all the nations" not for its own glory but "for praise and fame and honor" to God, as Jeremiah puts it (Jeremiah 13:11). Peter calls followers of Jesus "a chosen family, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people God has made his own" (1 Peter 2:9).
